title: Sorting materials: where to draw the line, and what a map of two numbers can show

summary.text: Weigh one katori of each of ten kitchen foods, and they line up in a ladder with no clear gap in the middle. So which foods are heavy and which are light? Anyone can draw the line anywhere. Then measure a second thing, how tall each food piles up, and put both numbers on a map. Sometimes the foods fall into clumps with empty space between them. Your child sorts dal by eye, in a hurry and with care, and counts the two kinds of mistake. They learn why a sorter can swap its mistakes but not remove them. They meet the astronomers who found whole families of stars by putting two numbers side by side. They also see why the groups we find depend on what we measure.
summary.art: A kitchen counter with ten katoris of different foods in a row and a hand-drawn map of dots beside them, with some dots drawn close together in rings.

intro.hook: Ten kitchen foods stand in a row: salt, sugar, rice, toor dal, mustard seeds, atta, maida, poha, ragi flour and sooji. Weigh one katori of each, and the weights make a ladder from the lightest food to the heaviest. There is no clear gap in the middle of it. Now, which of these foods are heavy foods, and which are light? Where does the line go?
intro.text: Nobody can say, because the ladder has no gap to show where to cut. You have to choose a line, and a friend can choose a different one. In this unit you find out how a line changes the groups, how a second number can show clumps that one number hides, and what happens when a sorter is hurried or strict. You also meet the astronomers who found the families of stars by doing exactly this.
intro.art: Ten katoris of kitchen foods lined up from lightest to heaviest, with a pencil line drawn across the row and a question mark above the line.

outcomes: I can put things in order by a number, draw a cut-off to make two groups, and say that the cut-off was my choice.
I can show that moving the cut-off moves some things into the other group while others never move.
I can plot two measurements for each thing on a map, and say whether the things fall into clumps with gaps.
I can explain that a gap on a map belongs to the numbers I chose as well as to the things, and that other numbers can give other groups.
I can count the mistakes a sorter makes, name the two kinds, and explain why moving the cut-off swaps one for the other.
I can sort at more than one level, lumping or splitting, and say which level suits which job.
I can give real examples of sorting by numbers, such as the star map, the plastic codes and rice grading.
I can say what computers can do with clumps in many numbers, and what is still argued about.

terms.meaning: Things lined up in order by a number, from the smallest to the biggest.
terms.example: Ten kitchen foods lined up from the lightest to the heaviest katori make a ladder.
terms.art: Ten katoris in a row, from the smallest to the biggest pile, with numbers beneath them.

terms.meaning: A number you choose to split a ladder into two groups. Things at or above it go in one group, and things below it go in the other.
terms.example: A college may say its cut-off is 90 marks. A student with 90 gets in, and a student with 89 does not.
terms.art: A ladder of ten things with a pencil line across it, labelled cut-off, and two groups named above and below.

terms.meaning: A number that says how much of something there is, with a unit such as grams or millimetres.
terms.example: One katori of rice has a mass of about 120 grams on a kitchen scale.
terms.art: A kitchen scale with a katori of rice on it and the number showing on the display.

terms.meaning: A picture that places each thing as a dot, using two numbers. Scientists call it a scatter plot.
terms.example: On the Katori Map, each food is a dot placed by its mass across and its heap height up.
terms.art: A square map with two axes and a dozen dots, each dot labelled with a food name.

terms.meaning: One of the two lines along the edges of a map. Each axis shows one measurement with a scale.
terms.example: On the Katori Map, the line along the bottom is the mass axis, and the line up the side is the heap height axis.
terms.art: A map with the bottom axis labelled mass in grams and the side axis labelled height in millimetres.

terms.meaning: A group of dots lying close together on a map. Scientists also call it a cluster.
terms.example: On the Katori Map, atta, maida and ragi flour may sit together in one clump.
terms.art: A map with three rings drawn round three groups of dots.

terms.meaning: An empty stretch on a map or a ladder with no dots in it.
terms.example: On a map of stars, there is a gap between the faint hot white dwarfs and the bright hot main sequence stars.
terms.art: A map with two clumps of dots and an empty space between them marked gap.

terms.meaning: A dot that sits far from all the others. It does not belong to any clump.
terms.example: Poha, light and flaky, may sit far from the other foods on the Katori Map.
terms.art: A map with a clump of dots and one dot far away from the rest, marked outlier.

terms.meaning: A mistake made by a sorter that holds back a thing that belongs in the group. It is also called a missed one.
terms.example: A good grain of toor dal that was left in the pile because the sorter was not sure of it.
terms.art: A toor dal piece left in the mixed pile while its group sits in a bowl nearby.

terms.meaning: A mistake made by a sorter that lets in a thing that does not belong to the group. It is also called a false alarm.
terms.example: A piece of chana dal that landed in the bowl for toor dal.
terms.art: A piece of chana dal sitting in a bowl full of toor dal.

terms.meaning: A change that makes one thing better and another thing worse at the same time. Moving the cut-off of a sorter is a trade-off between the two kinds of mistake.
terms.example: A stricter dal sorter lets fewer stones through but also throws away more good dal.
terms.art: A seesaw with wrongly kept back on one end and wrongly let through on the other.

terms.meaning: A flat tool with holes of one size. Small things pass through and big things stay on top.
terms.example: A chalni sorts fine flour from lumps in the kitchen.
terms.art: A round steel sieve with flour falling through and lumps staying on top.

terms.meaning: A step in sorting into groups inside groups. A coarse level has few big groups, and a fine level has many small groups.
terms.example: Metal is a coarse level, steel is a finer level, and stainless steel is finer still.
terms.art: A tree diagram with metal at the top, steel and brass below, and stainless steel below steel.

terms.meaning: Lumping means putting things into a few big groups. Splitting means putting them into many small groups.
terms.example: A spice shop might lump all seeds together, or split them into mustard, cumin, fennel and coriander.
terms.art: A spice shelf sorted two ways: one tray with all seeds mixed, and six small jars each with one kind of seed.

terms.meaning: A name for a group in a sorting by quality, such as grade A and grade B.
terms.example: Tea is sorted into grades by the size of the leaf pieces.
terms.art: Three bowls of tea leaves of different sizes labelled by grade.

terms.meaning: A small part taken from a big heap to find out about the whole heap.
terms.example: A trader takes one handful from a sack of rice to check how many grains are broken.
terms.art: A hand taking a handful of rice from the top of a full sack.

terms.meaning: The steepest slope that a heap of grains or powder can hold without sliding. A steeper heap has a bigger angle.
terms.example: A heap of mustard seeds is flatter than a heap of flour, so mustard has a smaller angle of repose.
terms.art: A cone-shaped heap of flour and a flatter heap of mustard seeds, each with its slope marked.

terms.meaning: A number from 1 to 7 inside a triangle of arrows that is stamped on many plastic things. It tells which kind of plastic the thing is made of.
terms.example: A clear drinking water bottle often has a 1 in the triangle, which means a plastic called PET.
terms.art: The bottom of a plastic bottle showing a triangle of arrows with the number 1 inside.

terms.meaning: The long band of dots on a star map where most stars lie. The stars on it are all burning hydrogen, and the hotter ones are brighter.
terms.example: The Sun is on the main sequence, with a yellow colour and middling brightness.
terms.art: A star map with a diagonal band of dots from faint red to bright blue, with the Sun marked in the middle.

terms.meaning: A small, hot, faint star. It is what is left when an ordinary star has used up its fuel and cast off its outer layers.
terms.example: Sirius B is a white dwarf that circles the bright star Sirius.
terms.art: A star map with one small white dot low on the hot side, labelled white dwarf, below the main sequence band.

explanations.concept: Sorting by a number: the ladder and the cut-off
explanations.definition: A ladder puts things in order by a number. A cut-off is a number chosen to split the ladder into two groups.
explanations.description: In the earlier unit on sorting, you sorted things by yes or no questions, such as hard or not hard. Many properties are not yes or no. How heavy is a katori of rice? It is a number, such as 120 grams. When you weigh ten foods, you can line them up from the lightest to the heaviest. That line is a ladder. To make two groups, you choose a cut-off. For example, you could say that any food at 100 grams or more is a heavy food. Everything on the ladder at 100 grams or more goes into one group. Everything below goes in the other. The ladder came from the foods. The cut-off came from you. A friend can choose 110 grams, and her groups will be different. Neither of you is wrong. Both are saying what you mean by heavy.
examples: A cut-off of 100 grams puts rice and dal in the heavy group, and a cut-off of 130 grams puts them in the light group.
A school may set a pass mark of 35 out of 100. A child with 35 passes, and a child with 34 does not.
A tea trader sorts leaf pieces into grades by size, and the lines between grades are chosen by the trade.
explanations.art: A ladder of ten foods with two pencil lines drawn at different heights, each line making a different pair of groups.

explanations.concept: Moving the cut-off: who moves and who never does
explanations.definition: When a cut-off moves, only the things close to it change group. Things far away from it stay in the same group, whatever sensible cut-off you pick.
explanations.description: Imagine a ladder of ten foods. In most kitchens, salt is the heaviest and poha is the lightest. If you draw the line anywhere in the middle, salt stays in the heavy group and poha stays in the light group. They are far from every sensible line. But a food in the middle, such as sooji, moves from one group to the other each time you slide the line past it. These are the borderline cases. They are the ones people argue about. You can measure how borderline a thing is. Ask ten people to draw their line, and count for each food how many put it in the heavy group. Salt will get ten out of ten and poha will get zero. Sooji might get five out of ten. A number from zero to ten tells you how sure the group is. This is better than just saying tricky. It also shows that the argument is about the line and not about the food.
examples: Salt and poha stay put whatever cut-off you choose, and foods in the middle of the ladder swap groups.
A student who scores 34 and a student who scores 36 are almost the same, but a pass mark of 35 puts them in different groups.
Five voters may put a rubber eraser in the soft group or the hard group, but all five put a steel katori in the hard group.
explanations.art: A ladder of ten foods with a shaded band in the middle labelled foods that change group, and the foods at the two ends labelled never change.

explanations.definition: A map of numbers, also called a scatter plot, shows each thing as a dot. One number decides how far across the dot is, and the other decides how far up.
explanations.description: A ladder uses one number. A map uses two. To make one, you measure two things about each food. You might measure the mass of a katori and the height of the heap it makes. Draw two lines, one along the bottom and one up the side. These are the axes. Put the mass along the bottom and the height up the side. Each food becomes one dot. Say sooji measures 100 grams and 33 millimetres. Its dot goes 100 grams across and 33 millimetres up. A map shows something that no ladder can. Two foods can be close on one number but far apart on the other. On the mass ladder, sugar and rice might sit side by side. On the map, they may be far apart if rice makes a flatter heap. So a map shows how things are alike in two ways at once.
examples: Each food is one dot placed by its mass and its heap height.
A map of children could place each child by height across and age up.
A map of stars places each star by colour across and brightness up.
explanations.art: A map with mass in grams along the bottom and heap height in millimetres up the side, with ten food dots labelled with their names.

explanations.concept: Clumps and gaps: groups that show themselves
explanations.definition: A clump is a set of dots lying close together on a map. A gap is an empty stretch between clumps. Scientists call this finding clusters.
explanations.description: When you put many things on a map, the dots do not always spread evenly. Sometimes they gather in clumps with empty space between them. Nobody drew those clumps. The numbers made them. On the Katori Map, the fine flours may all sit together, light and steep. The smooth round seeds may sit together, middling and flatter. Salt and sugar may form a third clump. Then you can draw a ring around each clump, and name the group. This is a very different way of making groups. On a ladder, you choose a line and the line makes the groups. On a map, the dots may show you the groups first, and then you draw the ring round what you see. Some dots stay alone. These are outliers. An outlier is not a mistake. It may be the most interesting dot on the map.
examples: Atta, maida and ragi flour may sit close together on the Katori Map.
Salt, sugar and rice may form a group of heavy, smooth crystals and grains.
Poha, light and flaky, may sit alone as an outlier.
explanations.art: A map of ten food dots with three rings drawn around three clumps and one dot outside the rings marked alone.

explanations.concept: Do the groups exist before we look for them?
explanations.description: Gaps on a map seem to show that nature has groups of its own. But the gap you see depends on the two numbers you chose. Measure other things about the same foods, and the dots may fall in different places, with different clumps and different gaps. So are the groups out there, or do we make them by choosing what to measure? Scientists and philosophers still argue about this. Some say that certain groups are real. For example, all gold atoms are exactly alike, and no gold atom sits half way to silver. Others say that most groups, such as a weed, a vegetable or a plastic, are made by us for our own purposes, and nature has no such boxes. Most people agree on a middle path. Nature has patterns, such as the gap between a faint white dwarf and a bright star. Which patterns we notice, and what we call them, depends on the questions we ask.
examples: All gold atoms are alike, so the group gold seems real.
A tomato is a fruit to a botanist and a vegetable to a cook.
A food can be in the clump of flours on one map and not on another.
explanations.art: Two maps of the same ten foods drawn with different pairs of numbers, with different clumps ringed on each.

perspectives.who: Scientists who think many groups are real
perspectives.explanation: Some groups are found in nature whatever we measure. All the atoms of one element are exactly alike, so the group is there before we look. Gaps that show up on many different maps are probably real.

perspectives.who: Scientists who think most groups are made by us
perspectives.explanation: Most groups depend on the numbers we pick and the lines we draw. A different question gives different groups. Nature has patterns, but the boxes are ours.

explanations.concept: The star map: Hertzsprung, Russell and the families of stars
explanations.definition: A star map, called the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram, places each star by its colour across and its brightness up. Most stars fall on a band called the main sequence, with giants above it and white dwarfs below it.
explanations.description: About 1900, astronomers at Harvard sorted thousands of stars by the dark lines in their light. Annie Jump Cannon led the sorting, and Antonia Maury added careful notes on how sharp the lines were. Their types were really a sorting by colour and surface heat. In the early 1900s, a Danish astronomer named Ejnar Hertzsprung noticed that among the red stars, some were enormously bright and others very faint, with few in between. In 1913, the American astronomer Henry Norris Russell showed a map that put brightness against type for many stars. The stars were not scattered everywhere. Most lay along a long band from hot and bright to cool and faint. Above the band sat bright cool giants, and below it sat faint hot white dwarfs. The map showed families of stars before anybody knew what made them different. Later, physics showed that the band is made of stars of different masses, all burning hydrogen. Cecilia Payne, in 1925, had shown that the types were really a ladder of temperature.
examples: The Sun sits in the middle of the main sequence.
Betelgeuse is a red giant, cool and very bright.
Sirius B is a white dwarf, hot and faint.
explanations.art: A star map with colour across and brightness up, showing a diagonal band of dots, a clump of giants above it and a single white dwarf below it.

explanations.concept: The map of materials: families that appear by themselves
explanations.definition: A materials chart, such as the Ashby chart, places materials by two properties, for example how heavy they are for their size and how stiff they are. Families of materials show up as clumps.
explanations.description: Starting around 1990, an engineer at Cambridge named Michael Ashby made charts for choosing materials. He plotted thousands of materials by two properties at a time, such as stiffness against density. On many of these charts, the materials fall into families. Metals sit in one clump, heavy and stiff. Woods and foams sit in another, light and less stiff. Plastics and rubbers sit in a third, light and soft. Glass and ceramics sit in a fourth, hard and brittle. Nobody told the dots where to go. The families are the ones people already knew from names like metal, plastic and wood, and the chart shows that those names mean something about the numbers. An engineer who needs something light and stiff finds that spot on the chart and reads off the materials near it. The empty parts of a chart are interesting too. They show what no known material does well, and they are where designers aim new materials.
examples: Steel and copper sit in the heavy, stiff clump.
Pine and bamboo sit near each other in the light clump.
Carbon-fibre materials sit in a place that is light and very stiff, where few older materials did.
explanations.art: A materials chart with four clumps labelled metals, woods and foams, plastics and rubbers, and glass and ceramics, and an empty corner marked wanted.

explanations.concept: Counting mistakes: two ways a sorter can be wrong
explanations.definition: A sorter can make two kinds of mistake. It can wrongly keep back a thing that belongs in the group, or it can wrongly let through a thing that does not belong.
explanations.description: Suppose you sort toor dal from a mix that also holds chana dal. Your toor dal bowl should hold only toor dal. If a piece of toor dal is left in the mixed heap, you have wrongly kept it back. If a piece of chana dal ends up in the toor bowl, you have wrongly let it through. These are two different mistakes, and you can count each one. Doctors do the same with a test for an illness. A test can miss a sick person, or it can say that a healthy person is sick. The two mistakes are counted separately because they cost different things. A rice mill that throws out good rice loses money. A rice mill that lets a stone through can break a customer's tooth. The mill must decide which mistake is worse, and set its sorter accordingly. Counting both kinds is the first step in judging any sorter.
examples: A piece of toor dal left in the mixed heap is wrongly kept back.
A piece of chana dal in the toor bowl is wrongly let through.
A smoke alarm that rings for toast is a false alarm. One that stays silent in a fire has missed the fire.
explanations.art: Two bowls: one for toor dal with a chana dal piece in it labelled wrongly let through, and a mixed heap with a toor dal piece in it labelled wrongly kept back.

explanations.concept: The trade-off: no cut-off removes both mistakes
explanations.definition: When two groups overlap on one number, moving the cut-off swaps one kind of mistake for the other. Only a better measurement can reduce both.
explanations.description: In the Strict and Relaxed test, a strict sorter takes only pieces she is sure of. She lets almost no wrong pieces in, but she leaves many good ones behind. A relaxed sorter takes everything that might be right. She leaves almost none behind, but she lets in many wrong pieces. Moving from strict to relaxed does not remove mistakes. It swaps one kind for the other. This happens whenever the two groups overlap on the thing you measure. A small chana dal may look just like a big toor dal. No cut-off on size can split them perfectly. To do better, you need a second number that separates them, such as colour or weight. With two numbers, the overlap may disappear. This is why real mills pass grain through several machines, each sorting by a different number. When one number leaves the groups overlapping, a cleverer cut-off will not fix it. A new number might.
examples: A strict sorter lets nothing wrong in, and wrongly keeps back many good pieces.
A relaxed sorter wrongly keeps back almost none, and lets many wrong pieces in.
A rice mill uses one machine for size, one for weight and one with a camera for colour.
explanations.art: A seesaw labelled wrongly kept back on one end and wrongly let through on the other, with a hand moving a cut-off marker underneath.

explanations.concept: Fast and careful: how sorters check their work
explanations.definition: Hurrying makes more mistakes, so careful sorters check a sample and sort in more than one stage.
explanations.description: A quick sort and a careful sort give different results. When you hurry, you make more mistakes of both kinds, because you glance at each piece for less time. Real sorting systems know this. A buyer does not look at every grain in a sack. She takes a sample, a small handful, and counts the broken or wrong grains in it. If the share of wrong grains in the sample is small, she assumes the sack is good. Mills also sort in stages. A fast, cheap first stage removes most of the rubbish. A slower, more careful stage works on what is left. This is cheaper than one slow stage for everything. A bigger sample gives a better guess, but it takes longer. So sorting is always a balance between speed, cost and the number of mistakes you can live with.
examples: A trader takes a handful from a sack to judge the whole sack.
A mill removes dust and big stones first, then uses a camera sorter on the cleaner rice.
A doctor may use a quick test first, and a slower, more exact test if the first one says maybe.
explanations.art: A rice mill with three stages in a row: a rough sieve, a stone remover and a camera sorter, with rice getting cleaner at each stage.

explanations.definition: Sorting can be done at different levels. Lumping uses a few big groups. Splitting uses many small groups, often inside the big ones.
explanations.description: You can sort the same spice shelf at several levels. At the coarsest level, you have one group, spices. One level finer, you can have seeds, powders and leaves. Finer still, you can have mustard, cumin, fennel and coriander seeds. A sorter who makes many small groups is called a splitter, and one who makes a few big groups is called a lumper. Charles Darwin wrote in a letter to a friend that it is good to have both hair-splitters and lumpers. Which level is right depends on the job. If you only need to know which jars go in the kitchen, seeds and powders is enough. If you need to find cumin in the dark, you need the finer level. Scientists use levels everywhere. Steel is a kind of metal, and stainless steel is a kind of steel. Linnaeus, a Swedish scientist, sorted living things into groups inside groups in the 1700s.
examples: Spices, then seeds, then mustard seeds, are three levels of the same shelf.
Metal, steel, and stainless steel are three levels of the same family.
Plastic, then the plastic called PET, is a finer level than just plastic.
explanations.art: A tree diagram of a spice shelf with spices at the top, then seeds powders and leaves, and then four jars of seeds below.

explanations.concept: Sorting plastics: the number in the triangle
explanations.definition: A resin code is a number from 1 to 7 stamped inside a triangle of arrows on plastic things. It names the family of plastic the thing is made from.
explanations.description: Turn over a plastic bottle, a curd cup or a tiffin box. Many have a small triangle of arrows with a number inside. This is a resin code. It started in the United States in 1988, to help sort plastics for recycling. A 1 means PET, the plastic of most clear drink bottles. A 2 means HDPE, used for milk cans and many caps. A 5 means polypropylene, used for many tiffin boxes and curd cups. A 7 means other, which is a box for everything that does not fit the first six. That makes it the tricky middle again. Recycling plants use the differences between plastics to sort them. For example, many of them put chopped plastic in a tank of water. Some plastics, such as HDPE and polypropylene, float, and others, such as PET, sink. The code tells you what the plastic is made of. It does not tell you whether your town can recycle it.
examples: A clear water bottle often has a 1 in the triangle.
A milk can or shampoo bottle often has a 2.
A box marked 7 may hold many different kinds of plastic.
explanations.art: The bottoms of four plastic things in a row, each with the triangle of arrows and a number, 1, 2, 5 and 7.

explanations.concept: Sorting by computers: clumps in many numbers
explanations.description: A human can draw a map of two numbers. A computer can find clumps among hundreds. In 1936, a British statistician named Ronald Fisher studied 150 iris flowers that an American botanist, Edgar Anderson, had measured four ways each. When he looked at the numbers, one kind of iris was cleanly separate. The other two kinds overlapped, so no cut-off on those four numbers could sort them without some mistakes. Today, computer programs sort photographs, voices and shopping habits in the same way. They look for clumps, or they learn a rule from examples. But they still need a person to decide which numbers to give them, and what the clumps mean. And they can make mistakes unevenly. In 2018, two researchers, Joy Buolamwini and Timnit Gebru, reported a problem. Several commercial computer systems tried to tell men from women in photographs. They made far more mistakes on darker-skinned women than on lighter-skinned men. Counting both kinds of mistake, for every group of people, is how such a problem is found.
examples: Fisher found that one kind of iris was cleanly separate and two overlapped.
A computer can find clumps among hundreds of numbers at once.
A sorter that works for most people can still make many more mistakes for some people.
explanations.art: A computer screen showing a cloud of coloured dots in three clumps, with two clumps overlapping and one standing apart.

agreed.text: When things are sorted by one number, the cut-off is a choice. Things near the cut-off change group when it moves, and things far from it never do.
agreed.evidence: Ten foods sorted by the mass of a katori gave the same two groups at the ends of the ladder whatever cut-off was used, and different groups in the middle.

agreed.text: A map of two numbers can show clumps and gaps that a ladder of one number hides.
agreed.evidence: On the star map, stars fall into a main sequence, giants and white dwarfs, though they form no clear groups on a ladder of brightness alone.

agreed.text: A sorter that uses one measurement on groups that overlap has to trade one kind of mistake for the other.
agreed.evidence: In the Strict and Relaxed test, the strict round left more good pieces behind and the relaxed round let in more wrong pieces.

agreed.text: The Hertzsprung–Russell diagram shows families of stars: the main sequence, giants and white dwarfs.
agreed.evidence: It has been drawn for many thousands of stars, using the measured brightness and colour of each.

agreed.text: Families of materials, such as metals, woods, plastics and ceramics, appear as clumps on charts that plot two properties.
agreed.evidence: Ashby's charts, built from the measured properties of thousands of materials.

agreed.text: Computers can find clumps in many numbers at once, but people choose the numbers and decide what the clumps mean.
agreed.evidence: Fisher's iris study in 1936, and tests of face-sorting systems that counted mistakes for each group of people.

challenging.claim: A group is found in nature. We do not make it.
challenging.who: Some scientists, and many people who learned sorting from a book.
challenging.for: All atoms of gold are alike, and stars fall in clear families on a map.
challenging.against: The gap you see depends on the numbers you measure. Another pair of numbers can give another set of groups. A group such as vegetable or weed is made by us for our own purposes.

challenging.claim: A careful enough sorter can have no mistakes.
challenging.for: A slow, careful sorter makes fewer mistakes, so it seems that enough care would remove them all.
challenging.against: If two groups overlap on the number you measure, no cut-off can separate them. Care moves the mistakes between the two kinds but does not remove them. Only a better measurement can.

challenging.claim: Things in the same clump are the same kind of thing.
challenging.who: Many people, and some early scientists.
challenging.for: Dots in a clump look alike, and the clump seems to be a natural kind.
challenging.against: A clump is alike only in the numbers that were used. Two foods in one clump on the Katori Map can differ in colour, taste and what they are used for. A different map would put them apart.

challenging.claim: A sorter that makes more mistakes is a worse sorter.
challenging.against: A strict sorter and a relaxed sorter can make the same total number of mistakes. They make different kinds, and one kind may cost far more. A smoke alarm should rather ring for toast than miss a fire.

challenging.claim: There is one right number of groups for any set of things.
challenging.for: A set of things seems to have natural boundaries.
challenging.against: Lumpers and splitters sort the same things into fewer or more groups, and each can be useful. The right level depends on the job.

challenging.claim: A computer sorts without bias because it only uses numbers.
challenging.for: A computer follows fixed rules, so it seems fair.
challenging.against: Researchers have shown that some computer systems made far more mistakes on some groups of people than on others. The numbers chosen and the examples used to train the system can carry a bias.

big_questions.q: The ladder of foods had no gap, yet people drew lines anyway. Is a line something nature gives us, or something we make?
big_questions.hint: Think about the pass mark in a test and about the exact moment a child becomes an adult.

big_questions.q: Two numbers showed clumps that one number hid. What might a third number show?
big_questions.hint: Think about the foods and what else you could measure about them, such as how they taste or how they cook.

big_questions.q: A smoke alarm that never misses a fire will sometimes ring for toast. Which mistake would you rather it make, and who should decide?
big_questions.hint: Count the cost of each mistake, not just how many there are.

big_questions.q: A pass mark of 35 means that 34 fails and 35 passes. What is the real difference between those two children?
big_questions.hint: Think about how a line on a ladder treats people who are almost the same.

big_questions.q: A computer that tried to tell men from women in photographs made more mistakes on some groups of people than on others. Where could those mistakes come from, and how would you find them?
big_questions.hint: Think about the examples it learned from, and about counting mistakes for each group.

big_questions.q: Annie Jump Cannon sorted stars by their light, and Hertzsprung and Russell put brightness next to that sort. Why do new answers so often come from putting two old sorts side by side?
big_questions.hint: Think of what a map shows that a ladder cannot.

big_questions.q: Should a sorter ever be allowed to say that it is not sure? What would we need to change if it could?
big_questions.hint: Think of the unsure bowl in a sorting test and what happens to the pieces in it.

big_questions.q: On a map, the dots made clumps that we did not draw. Does that mean the groups were already in the foods, or did our two numbers make them?
big_questions.hint: Think about what would happen on a map made from two different numbers.

big_questions.q: Many languages have fewer or more words for colours than others, and draw the line between blue and green at different places. Is the colour line in the world, or in the people?
big_questions.hint: Think about a ladder of colours with no gaps and about who needs the line.

story.title: The Dial on the Machine
story.note: A made-up story. Rice mills in the Thanjavur region, machines with cameras and puffs of air that push out bad grains, and machines that remove stones by weight are all real. The mill, the people and the map in the story are imagined.
text: Kamala Athai's rice mill stood at the end of a long road through the paddy fields near Thanjavur. In the week before Pongal, it never stopped. Lorries came in with sacks of rice. Lorries went out with sacks of rice. Meenakshi, who was ten, spent her holidays there, sitting on an upturned bucket and watching.

This year there was something new in the mill. It was a tall grey machine with a camera inside and a small dial on the front. Rice poured in at the top. The camera looked at every grain as it fell. If a grain looked wrong, a tiny puff of air blew it into a side bin. Good rice fell into the front bin.

'What is the dial for?' asked Meenakshi. 'It says how strict the machine is,' said her cousin Karthik. He was fourteen, and he had been trusted to run it. 'Turn it up, and the machine throws out more.'

The trouble began on the second day. A customer in Kumbakonam telephoned. She had bitten on a small stone in her rice, and it had hurt her tooth. Kamala Athai frowned. 'Make the machine stricter,' she said. Karthik turned the dial up.

On the third day, the side bin was full to the brim. Meenakshi looked into it. Most of what lay there was good white rice, with a chalky spot or a slightly different shade. Kamala Athai looked at the bin, and then at her account book. 'At this rate,' she said, 'we throw away more than we sell.' She told Karthik to turn the dial down.

On the fourth day, a stone got through again. Kamala Athai said nothing for a long time. She had turned the dial up, and she had turned it down, and each time she had swapped one trouble for the other.

Meenakshi had learned at school that week how to count the mistakes of a sorter. She asked the kitchen for two cups. She took a handful from the side bin and a handful from the front bin. Then she sat on her bucket and counted. In the front bin, a few stones. In the side bin, many good grains. She wrote two columns in her notebook.

'The dial does not take the mistakes away,' she said slowly. 'It only moves them. Strict has fewer stones and more thrown-away rice. Loose has more stones and less thrown-away rice. It is a seesaw.' Karthik rolled his eyes. 'Then how do you fix a seesaw?' 'You don't push it,' said Meenakshi. 'You look at something else.'

She laid thirty things on a newspaper: ten stones from the bin, ten chalky grains and ten good grains. She looked at them very hard. By colour, the stones and the chalky grains looked almost the same, pale and dull. That was why the camera could not tell them apart. But when she held a stone in one hand and a chalky grain in the other, one felt like nothing, and the other felt like a tiny weight.

She borrowed the little scale from the tea shop and weighed the things in tens. Then she drew a map. Across the page went how pale a thing was. Up the page went how heavy it was. She put a dot for every one of the thirty things.

The dots fell into three small clumps. The good grains sat low down on one side. The chalky grains sat low down on the other. The stones sat high above both, with a clear gap of empty paper between. 'Look,' said Meenakshi. 'The camera cannot find the stones by colour. A scale finds them at once.'

Kamala Athai looked at the map for a long time. 'There is an old machine in the back shed,' she said. 'It shakes the rice on a sloping tray with a little wind. The heavy things stay on the tray, and the light rice floats off. We never used it, because the new machine had a camera.' Karthik fetched it. They put it first in the line, and the camera second. Meenakshi turned the dial of the camera back to its middle.

By Pongal morning, the stones were gone from the front bin, and the side bin was nearly empty. The camera now threw out only the chalky grains that it was meant to find. Kamala Athai tore the page from Meenakshi's notebook and pinned it beside the machine.

'Why did it work?' asked Karthik. 'One number could not split them,' said Meenakshi. 'Two numbers could.' She looked at the pinned page. Three clumps and a gap. The grains had never been the problem. The problem was the way they had been looked at.
Outside, the first pots of Pongal were beginning to boil over in the courtyards of the village. Not one of them held a stone.
story.epiphany: A dial can only swap one kind of mistake for the other. When two groups look alike on one number, a second number can pull them apart into clumps with a gap between.
ask: Why did turning the dial up, and then down, not solve the trouble at the mill?
Why could the camera not tell the stones from the chalky grains, when a scale could?
Can you think of another job where one measurement is not enough, and a second one would help?

A tall grey machine with a camera window and a small dial, and a side bin full of white rice beside it.
A girl on an upturned bucket drawing a map of dots in a notebook, with three small heaps on a newspaper beside her.

games.title: Where Is the Line?
games.players: 2 to 4 players, or one child playing against a grown-up
games.context: This is a guessing game about cut-offs. Every card has a squish score. One player secretly picks a cut-off between squishy and firm, and the others ask questions to find it.

setup.art: Twenty-four cards laid in a row on a table from the highest squish score to the lowest, forming a ladder, with a Yes row and a No row above.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards and lay them in a ladder, from the highest score to the lowest.

setup.art: A Judge writing a secret number on a slip of paper and folding it, while the other players watch the ladder.
setup.caption: 2. The Judge writes a secret cut-off number and folds the slip.

setup.art: A guesser pointing at the card in the middle of the ladder and asking the Judge if it is squishy, with the answer moving the card to the Yes row.
setup.caption: 3. Guessers ask about one card at a time. The Judge says yes or no.

printables.title: 24 two-sided cards: a thing with its squish score on the front, and a line about why on the back

items.b: Very squishy. It is mostly air between soft fibres, so it squashes almost flat.
Very squishy. It is full of tiny air pockets that squash and then spring back.
Very squishy. The stuffing is mostly air between fluffy fibres.
Very squishy. A sponge is full of holes that squash flat and then open again.
Squishy. The loops of cotton and the air between them squash under a hand.
Squishy. A fresh idli is a light, airy cake that dents under a finger.
Fairly squishy. Bread has many small holes made by gas, and they squash.
Fairly squishy. The flesh dents under a thumb.
Fairly squishy. Dough squashes and stays squashed, instead of springing back.
Middling. Clay squashes under a firm push and keeps its new shape.

items.f: Butter on a warm day. Squish score 10.
items.b: Middling. On a warm day in Chennai, butter is soft. On a cold day it is much harder.
Middling to firm. Rubber squashes a little and then springs back.
Middling to firm. An eraser dents a little under a fingernail and springs back.

items.f: Empty plastic bottle with the cap on. Squish score 6.
items.b: Middling to firm. The thin walls squeeze in easily, and the air inside pushes them back.
Firm. Wax holds its shape, but a fingernail leaves a small mark.
Firm. A thumb does not dent a fresh apple.
Firm. A raw potato stays hard under a thumb.
Very firm. Wood does not dent under a thumb or a fingernail.
Very firm. It is dry and crisp, and it snaps instead of squashing.
Very firm. Wood and graphite do not squash under a finger.
Rock hard. Steel does not dent under any push a hand can make.
Rock hard. Glass does not dent, though it may break.
Rock hard. A brick does not squash under any hand.
Rock hard. A fired clay cup does not dent.

rules: The squish score is a score made up for this game. It goes from 1, rock hard, to 20, very squishy. The order of the cards is roughly right.
One player is the Judge. The Judge secretly writes a cut-off number between 6 and 15 on a slip of paper and folds it.
Squishy means a squish score at or above the cut-off. Everything below it is firm.
The other players take turns to point at one card and ask, 'Is this card squishy?' The Judge says yes or no, using the cut-off.
Each guesser asks two questions. Then each guesser secretly writes down a guess for the cut-off number.
The Judge opens the slip. A guess that is exactly right wins 3 tokens. A guess one away wins 2 tokens. A guess two away wins 1 token.
The Judge wins 1 token for each guesser who is three or more away. Then the next player becomes the Judge. After everyone has been the Judge once, the player with the most tokens wins.
If you run out of tokens, keep the score on paper.

flow.do: Cut out the 24 cards and the 20 tokens. Lay the cards in a row, from the highest squish score to the lowest. Check that the order is a ladder.
flow.say: These cards have squish scores from 1 to 20. We lay them in a row from the highest to the lowest. That makes a ladder.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Lay them in a row from 20 down to 1.
flow.context: This is the first step of Where Is the Line? You set up the cards and make the ladder.
flow.parent: Young children can ask a grown-up to cut with scissors. No printer? Write each card's name and score on a slip of paper. The back lines are not needed to play. With only two players, the child can be the Judge first so a grown-up has to guess.

flow.do: Play a practice round. You are the Judge, with a secret cut-off of 10. Ask your child to ask about one card at a time. Show how each answer moves a card to the Yes row or the No row.
flow.say: I have a secret cut-off. A card with a score at or above it is squishy. Point at a card and ask me if it is squishy. Which card will you ask about first? Why?
flow.kid: Pick one card. Ask the Judge if it is squishy. Which card first, and why?

ask.q: Which card would you ask about first, and why?
good: The one in the middle of the ladder.
The one at the middle, because it cuts the ladder in half.
One near the middle, so each answer rules out a lot.

flow.parent: A good first question is a card from the middle of the ladder. Whatever the answer, half of the cards are ruled out. Do not tell your child this. Let them find it, and ask why after the round.
flow.context: In this step, you learn the game with a practice round.

flow.do: Play round one. A new Judge writes a secret cut-off. Each guesser asks two questions, writes a guess, and then the Judge opens the slip. Hand out tokens as the rules say.
flow.say: Judge, write your secret number. Guessers, ask two questions each. Then write your guess. Let us see who is closest.
flow.kid: Play a round. Ask two questions. Write your guess for the cut-off.

ask.q: What helped you make a good guess?
good: Asking about a card in the middle first.
Asking about cards close to the answers I already had.
Watching which cards moved to the Yes row.

flow.context: In this step, you play a full round and score it.

flow.do: Swap the Judge and play round two. After the round, point at the two cards on each side of the real cut-off. Ask what the difference between them really is.
flow.say: New Judge, new round. After this one, look at the two cards on either side of the cut-off. How different are they really?
flow.kid: Swap the Judge. Play round two. Look at the two cards next to the cut-off.
flow.parent: This is the heart of the game. Cards next to the line are almost the same, yet they land in different groups. Cards far from the line never change.

check.q: The Judge's cut-off was 10. The card with score 10 is squishy, and the card with score 8 is firm. What does this show?
options: The two cards are almost the same, and the line was the Judge's choice
The cut-off is a fact about the cards
The card with 9 is much harder than the card with 10
check.why: A score of 10 and a score of 8 are close. The Judge could have put the cut-off a step or two higher, and the card with 10 would have joined the firm group. The line was the Judge's choice and not a fact about the cards.

flow.context: In this step, you play a second round and look closely at the line.

flow.do: Count the tokens and name the winner. Then ask which cards were never in doubt, and which cards changed groups from round to round.
flow.say: Count your tokens. Now think. Which cards stayed in the same group in every round? Which cards changed?
flow.kid: Count your tokens. Which cards always stayed put? Which ones moved?

ask.q: Which cards never changed group, whatever the cut-off?
good: The ones at the very top and the very bottom.
The very squishy and the rock hard ones.
The ones far from the middle.

flow.context: In this step, you finish the game and talk about which cards moved.

items.p: Ten foods are lined up by the mass of one katori, with no clear gap in the middle of the ladder. Someone says that heavy foods start at 100 grams. Which statement is true?
opts: The ladder itself shows where the line must go
The line at 100 grams is a choice, and another person could choose another line
The foods decide where the line goes
There is only one correct line
items.why: A ladder with no gap gives no sign of where to cut. The cut-off comes from the person who chooses it. Another sensible person could choose 110 grams, and get different groups.

items.p: A number chosen to split a ladder of things into two groups is called a ____.
items.why: A cut-off is chosen by the sorter. Things at or above it go in one group, and things below it go in the other.

items.p: If you move a cut-off a little, every thing on the ladder changes group.
items.why: False. Only the things close to the cut-off change group. Things far from it stay in the same group, whatever sensible cut-off you pick.

items.p: Put these steps for making a map of numbers in the right order.
items: Measure two numbers for each thing
Put a dot for each thing
items.a: order shown
items.why: You need the measurements first. Then you need the axes to place them on. Then each thing becomes a dot, and only then can you look for clumps and gaps.

items.p: Match each word to its meaning.
pairs: Things in order by a number
A number chosen to split a ladder in two
Dots lying close together on a map
An empty stretch with no dots
A dot far from all the others
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These five words are the vocabulary of sorting by numbers. A ladder uses one number, and a map of numbers uses two, so clumps, gaps and outliers appear only on a map.

items.p: Which of these are mistakes that wrongly keep back, and which wrongly let through? Sort them.
items: A good toor dal piece left in the mixed heap
Good rice thrown into the reject bin
A chana dal piece in the toor bowl
A pebble in the rice bag after sorting
items.a: see items
items.why: Wrongly kept back means a thing that belongs in the good group was held out of it. Wrongly let through means a thing that does not belong got in. The two kinds cost different things, so we count them separately.

items.p: A strict sorter takes only the pieces she is very sure about. Which kind of mistake will she make most of?
opts: Wrongly letting in pieces that do not belong
items.why: A strict sorter holds back every piece she is not sure of. That means she leaves many good pieces behind. She lets in almost no wrong pieces. Picking 'neither kind' forgets that no sorter on overlapping groups is perfect.

items.p: Look at the table. Which two foods would sit closest together on the map?
items.why: Rice and toor dal have the same mass, 120 grams, and heap heights only 2 millimetres apart. The other pairs differ by a lot in mass or in height or both.
items.context: In the Katori Map test, you weigh one katori of each food and measure the height of its heap. Here are made-up results for six foods.

chart.title: Made-up example: six foods on the Katori Map

items.p: A friend says that the line between heavy foods and light foods is in the foods themselves. Use the idea of a ladder to explain why the line is a choice.
items.a: A strong answer says that the foods make a ladder with no gap, so nothing in the foods shows where to cut. The line comes from whoever draws it, and a different person can draw another line and make different groups. Only the foods near the line change group. Salt and poha stay put whatever line is chosen.
items.why: The ladder does not show a gap, so the line must be put there by a person. The foods near the line are the ones whose group depends on the choice.

items.p: On a star map with colour across and brightness up, where do most stars lie?
opts: Spread evenly all over the map
In a long band from faint and red to bright and blue
items.why: Most stars fall along a long band called the main sequence. The Sun is on it. A few stars sit above it, the giants, and a few sit below, the white dwarfs. The stars are not spread evenly, which is what makes the families visible.

items.p: Here is a map of eight food dots. Label the three marked places with the words clump, gap or outlier.
labels: The ring round the three dots close together
The empty space between the two groups of dots
The single dot far from all the others
a: The ring round the three dots: clump
The empty space between the groups: gap
The single dot far away: outlier
items.why: A clump is dots lying close together. A gap is the empty space between clumps. An outlier is a dot far from the others.
items.art: A map with eight dots: three close together inside a ring, four in another group, one far away on its own, and an empty gap between the two groups.

items.p: Draw a ladder of five things you know, in order by a number. Draw two different cut-offs on it, and show how each one makes different groups.
items.a: A ladder of five things in order, such as five children by height, or five foods by mass. Two lines drawn across it at different places, with the groups named on each side. At least one thing changes group between the two lines.
items.why: Moving the line moves the things nearest to it from one group to the other.
items.art: A blank space for drawing a column of five boxes in order, with room beside it for two lines.

items.p: Three of these are levels of the same family. Which is the odd one out?
items.why: Metal, steel and stainless steel are groups inside groups: stainless steel is a kind of steel, and steel is a kind of metal. Plastic is a different family.

items.p: A tray holds 20 toor dal. After a strict round, 9 toor dal are in the toor bowl. How many toor dal were wrongly kept back?
items.why: There were 20 toor dal. 9 are in the bowl. 20 take away 9 is 11. So 11 toor dal were wrongly kept back.

items.p: Two foods in the same clump on one map must be the same kind of food.
items.why: False. Two foods in one clump are alike only in the two numbers that were plotted. They can differ in colour, taste and use. On a map made of other numbers, they might land far apart.

items.p: A plastic bottle has the number 2 inside a triangle of arrows. What does this tell you?
opts: It can be recycled in every town
It is made of one particular family of plastic
It is stronger than a bottle marked 1
It was made in the year 2
items.why: The number names the family of plastic, which for 2 is HDPE. It does not say whether your town can recycle it, or how strong it is.

items.p: Two groups of dal overlap in size, so some small pieces of one are as big as some big pieces of the other. What is true of a sorter that uses size alone?
opts: A careful enough cut-off sorts them perfectly
Size cannot be used to sort
The mistakes will all be of one kind
No cut-off on size can sort them without some mistakes
items.why: If the groups overlap on a number, any cut-off puts some pieces in the wrong group. A better cut-off only shifts which pieces are wrong. To do better, you need a second number.

items.p: A sorter is changed from strict to relaxed. What happens to her mistakes?
opts: Both kinds of mistake go down
Both kinds of mistake go up
Fewer pieces are wrongly kept back, and more are wrongly let through
items.why: A relaxed sorter takes everything that might be right. She leaves few good pieces behind, but she lets in more wrong ones. The mistakes are swapped, not removed.

items.p: In a relaxed round, 30 pieces are in the toor bowl and 11 of them are chana dal. The mix had 20 toor dal. How many toor dal are in the bowl, and how many toor dal were wrongly kept back?
items.a: 19 toor dal in the bowl, and 1 wrongly kept back
items.why: 30 pieces take away the 11 chana dal leaves 19 toor dal in the bowl. 20 toor dal take away 19 leaves 1 toor dal wrongly kept back.

items.p: Counting both kinds of mistake is the first step in judging any ____.
items.why: A sorter can fail in two ways. If you count only one kind, a sorter that takes everything or takes nothing can look perfect.

items.p: A rice mill must choose how strict to set its sorting machine. Three people give advice.

views.says: I never want a stone in my rice. Set the machine to be very strict.
A strict machine throws out too much good rice. We lose money.
Use a second machine that looks at a different thing, such as weight, and keep the first one in the middle.

items.ask: Which advice do you agree with most? Give a reason that uses the two kinds of mistake. Then say one thing that another person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks one piece of advice and says which mistake it reduces and which it increases. For example, the cook's idea of a second measurement could reduce both kinds. It then admits a fair point from someone else, such as the customer's wish for no stones, or the accountant's worry about waste.
items.why: Nobody is wrong. A strict setting protects customers but wastes rice. A second measurement may help with both. The right choice depends on which mistake costs more.

items.p: Explain why a second number can separate two groups that one number cannot. Use an example, and say what the map would look like.
items.a: A strong answer says that two groups can overlap on one number, such as colour, so no cut-off on colour can sort them. A second number, such as weight, may put the groups far apart. On a map of both numbers, the two groups would fall into two clumps with a gap, even though they overlap along each number alone. An example is stones and chalky rice grains, which look alike but differ in weight.
items.why: One number can hide the difference. Two numbers can pull the groups apart on a map.

items.p: Match each real sorter to the number or property it uses.
pairs: A colour sorter with a camera
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Every sorter uses a rule on a measurement. A sieve uses size, winnowing uses weight, a magnet uses a magnetic property and a camera uses colour.

items.p: Which of these are lines drawn by people on a number, and which are groups that do not depend on a line? Sort them.
cats: Does not depend on a line
items: A pass mark of 35 out of 100
An age limit for a ride
All atoms of gold being alike
Does not depend on a line
A coin landing heads or tails
Does not depend on a line
A seed sprouting or not sprouting
Does not depend on a line
items.a: see items
items.why: A pass mark, a cut-off list and an age limit are all chosen lines on a number. A coin landing heads or tails and a seed sprouting are two outcomes without any chosen line. All gold atoms are alike whatever we choose to measure.

items.p: A spice seller wants to find cumin quickly in a dark shop. Which way of sorting suits her best?
opts: Many small groups, one for each spice
Two big groups, seeds and powders
items.why: A fine level lets her go straight to the right jar. A coarse level would leave her searching through many jars. The best level depends on the job.

items.p: A Danish astronomer noticed that among red stars, some were extremely bright and others very faint. What did this suggest?
opts: Stars of the same colour can be very different in brightness, so there are different kinds of stars
All red stars are the same
items.why: Same colour but very different brightness meant that colour alone did not sort the stars into kinds. The stars fell into families that needed two numbers to see.

items.p: Put these steps in the order that finds families in a pile of things.
items: Measure two numbers for each thing
Plot the dots on a map
Ask why the things in a clump are alike
items.a: order shown
items.why: First you measure. Then you plot. Then you notice a pattern. Only then can you ask what causes it.

items.p: A recycling plant puts chopped plastic in a tank of water. Some pieces float and some sink. What is the plant doing?
opts: Sorting by a property that differs between plastics, how heavy they are for their size
items.why: Different plastics have different densities, so some float and some sink. The plant uses this difference as a rule, which is cheap and works on huge piles.

items.p: Invent five foods and two numbers for each. Draw a map of the five dots, label the axes, and ring any clump you find.
items.a: A map with two labelled axes, five dots each with a food name, and a ring round any dots that sit close together. The numbers must be plausible for the foods.
items.why: This checks that the child can make a map from two numbers and can spot a clump.
items.art: A blank square with space to draw two axes.

items.p: Here is a picture of a toor dal bowl with a chana dal piece in it, and a mixed heap with a toor dal piece in it. Label the two mistakes.
labels: The chana dal piece in the toor bowl
The toor dal piece in the mixed heap
a: The chana dal piece in the toor bowl: wrongly let through
The toor dal piece in the mixed heap: wrongly kept back
items.why: A piece that does not belong but got in is wrongly let through. A piece that does belong but was left out is wrongly kept back.
items.art: A bowl of toor dal with one chana dal piece among them, and a mixed heap of dal next to it with one toor dal piece arrowed.

items.p: A computer system that makes few mistakes overall can still make many mistakes on one group of people.
items.why: True. An overall count can hide big differences. In 2018, researchers reported that some face-sorting systems made far more mistakes on darker-skinned women than on lighter-skinned men. Counting mistakes for each group is how to find this.

items.p: In 1936, Ronald Fisher studied four measurements of 150 iris flowers. One kind separated cleanly, but two kinds overlapped. So no cut-off on those four numbers could sort the two overlapping kinds without some mistakes.
items.why: True. When two groups overlap on every number you have measured, mistakes are unavoidable. Only a new measurement might separate them.

items.p: Look at the chart. It shows made-up results from the Strict or Relaxed test. What does it suggest?
opts: The two rounds were exactly the same
Moving from strict to relaxed swapped one kind of mistake for the other
The relaxed round made no mistakes
The strict round made more mistakes of both kinds
items.why: In the strict round, 11 pieces were wrongly kept back and none wrongly let through. In the relaxed round, 1 was wrongly kept back and 11 were wrongly let through. The mistakes swapped.
items.context: In the Strict or Relaxed test, you sort a mix of toor dal and chana dal twice. You count the two kinds of mistake in each round.

chart.title: Made-up example: mistakes in two rounds of sorting dal
chart.x: Kind of mistake in each round
chart.note: These numbers are made up to show what results can look like. Your numbers will be different.

items.p: A mill's strict setting throws out 30 good grains in every 1000 and lets 0 stones through. Its loose setting throws out 2 good grains and lets 1 stone through. A stone costs 10 points and a thrown-out grain costs 1 point. Which setting costs less?
items.why: The strict setting costs 30 times 1, which is 30 points. The loose setting costs 2 times 1 plus 1 times 10, which is 12 points. So the loose setting costs less, though it lets a stone through. The cost of each kind of mistake decides.

items.p: A school sets a pass mark of 35 out of 100. Explain, using ideas from this unit, what the cut-off does to one child who scores 34 and another who scores 35.
items.a: A strong answer says that the pass mark is a cut-off chosen by people. The two children are almost the same on the ladder of marks, but the line puts them in different groups. Children far from the line, such as 10 or 90, would stay in the same group whatever sensible pass mark was chosen. It may add that the pass mark does not show whether either child understood the topic.
items.why: A cut-off puts nearly identical things in different groups. Those near the line are the ones whose group is a result of the choice.

items.p: Three scientists talk about the groups we find in nature.

views.says: All gold atoms are exactly alike. The group gold is there whether or not anybody draws a line.
Weed is just a plant in a place where somebody does not want it. Nature has no weeds.
Stars fall in families on the map whatever we do. But the names are ours, and the families depend on what we measure.

items.ask: Are the groups in the world, or are they made by us? Give a reason that uses something you found in this unit. Then say one thing that another person has right.
items.a: A strong answer may take either side or the middle, and gives a reason from the unit, such as the gap in the star map, the dependence of clumps on the numbers plotted, or the pass mark as a chosen line. It then admits a fair point from another person.
items.why: Some groups are likely real and some are made by us. Which is which depends on whether the group stays when we change what we measure.

items.p: A computer system sorts photographs of people. A researcher wants to know if it is fair. What is the best thing to do?
opts: Count the mistakes for everybody together
Count both kinds of mistake separately for each group of people
Ask the computer if it is fair
items.why: An overall count can hide a large difference between groups. Counting both kinds of mistake for each group is how researchers found uneven mistakes in face-sorting systems.

items.p: On the map, flour is at 80 grams and 48 millimetres high, and maida is at 80 grams and 51 millimetres high. How many millimetres higher is the maida heap than the flour heap?
items.a: 3 millimetres
items.why: Both are at 80 grams, so they are in the same place across. 51 take away 48 is 3. So maida is 3 millimetres higher, and the two dots sit very close together.

items.p: A ladder of foods by katori mass has these masses in grams: 60, 80, 80, 95, 100, 105, 120, 120, 128 and 180. Put these cut-offs in order from the one that makes the most foods heavy to the one that makes the fewest: 70, 100, 125, 150.
items.a: order shown
items.why: A low cut-off puts many foods above it. At 70, nine foods are heavy. At 100, six are heavy. At 125, two are heavy. At 150, only the 180 gram food is heavy.

items.p: Which is the better way to judge two sorters?
opts: Pick the one that looks neater
Count both kinds of mistake for each, and ask which kind costs more
Pick the one that is faster
Pick the one with the lower total of mistakes, whatever they are
items.why: Two sorters can make the same total of mistakes and still differ a great deal, because one kind of mistake can cost far more. Counting both kinds and weighing their cost is the fair way to judge.

items.p: Match each situation to the kind of mistake it shows.
pairs: A stone in a bag of rice
A good grain in the reject bin
A smoke alarm that rings for toast
A smoke alarm that stays silent in a real fire
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: A thing that does not belong but gets in is wrongly let through, like toast treated as fire. A thing that does belong but is held out is wrongly kept back, like a real fire that gets no alarm.

items.p: Which of these are finer levels of sorting, and which are coarser levels? Sort them.
items.a: see items
items.why: Metal, plastic and wood are broad families. Stainless steel, PET and teak are particular kinds inside them. Finer levels have more, smaller groups.

items.p: Give an example from your own life of a sort where moving the cut-off would swap mistakes. Say which mistake would cost more, and why.
items.a: A strong answer names a real sort, such as a smoke alarm, a school entry age, a lift weight limit or a test for illness. It says which mistake a stricter or a looser cut-off would increase, and gives a reason why one costs more, for example because a missed fire is worse than toast.
items.why: Every sort with a cut-off swaps one kind of mistake for the other. Deciding which is worse is a choice about costs.

items.p: A student looks at a map with two clumps and a wide gap, and says that the gap proves nature has two kinds. What is the best reply?
opts: The student is right, because gaps always show real groups
The gap belongs to these two numbers, so try another pair of numbers for the same things
items.why: A gap on a map is a fact about the numbers plotted. A different pair of numbers might fill it in, or show a different gap. Checking with other numbers tells you if the group is robust.

items.p: Draw a seesaw. Label one end wrongly kept back and the other wrongly let through. Show a hand moving a cut-off marker underneath, and what happens to the seesaw.
items.a: A seesaw with the two kinds of mistake on the two ends, a cut-off marker under it, and the seesaw tipped one way. Moving the marker tips the seesaw the other way. One kind goes down and the other goes up.
items.why: A picture of the trade-off helps you remember that moving the cut-off swaps the mistakes.
items.art: A blank space with a triangle drawn in the middle for the seesaw to balance on.

items.p: Why do astronomers draw a map of stars rather than just writing a list?
opts: Stars are easier to draw than to write
A map can show families that a list hides
items.why: A list of numbers does not show that the stars gather in a band, with giants above it and white dwarfs below it. A map does. Families are visible only when two numbers are put side by side.

items.p: A small handful taken from a big sack to find out what the whole sack is like is called a ____.
items.why: A sample lets you judge a big heap without checking every grain. A bigger sample gives a better guess but takes longer.

items.p: A very slow, careful sorter will make no mistakes if the two groups overlap on the number she measures.
items.why: False. If the groups overlap, no cut-off can separate them. Care changes which mistakes are made, but cannot remove them. Only a new measurement can.

items.p: Two groups overlap on every number you can measure. What is the best you can do?
opts: Accept some mistakes, and set the cut-off by which kind of mistake costs more
items.why: When the groups overlap on everything you can measure, mistakes cannot be avoided. The cut-off then decides which kind you accept, and the right choice depends on which kind costs more.

experiments.title: The Katori Map: two numbers for ten kitchen foods
experiments.question: If you sort ten kitchen foods by the mass of one katori, is there a gap in the ladder? And if you also measure how tall each food piles up, do the foods fall into clumps?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which food will be the heaviest in a katori, and which the lightest? Which will make the tallest heap? Will any foods sit close together on both counts? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: You use the same katori, filled level to the top, for every food. You pour each food from the same height onto the same plate, slowly. You measure each heap in the same way. Only the food changes, so any difference in mass or in heap height comes from the food.
results_table: Mass of one katori in grams
Height of the heap in millimetres, first pour
Height of the heap in millimetres, second pour

materials.item: 1 steel katori or small cup, the same one for every food
about one katori each of ten dry foods: salt, sugar, raw rice, toor dal, mustard seeds, atta, maida, poha, ragi flour and sooji
closed jars, boxes or the food's own packets, to keep each food dry and to pour it back into
a kitchen scale that shows grams, or a neighbour's or a kirana shop's scale
a ruler marked in millimetres
a flat, smooth plate or tray, with no rim in the middle
the flat back of a steel spoon or a ruler, for levelling the top of the katori
newspaper to spread under the plate
graph paper, or plain paper with a grid drawn on it, a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: Do not eat the foods in this test. Flour dust can make you sneeze, so pour slowly and keep your face away. Leave out any food that your child is allergic to, and use another dry food from the kitchen. Wash your hands after the test. Keep small grains and seeds away from the mouths and noses of little brothers and sisters. A grown-up should help anyone under six.
experiments.record: For each food, write the mass of one katori and two heap heights. Then find the average height. Last, draw the map, with one dot for each food, and ring the clumps you see.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you weigh one katori of each of ten foods and measure how tall each food piles up. Then you draw a map with both numbers and look for clumps.

setup.art: A steel katori filled level with rice on a kitchen scale showing a number in grams.
setup.caption: 1. Fill the katori level with a food. Weigh it and write the grams.

setup.art: Ten foods written in a column in order from lightest to heaviest, with a pencil line drawn across it at one place.
setup.caption: 2. Make a ladder from lightest to heaviest. Draw a line where you think heavy foods begin.

setup.art: A hand holding a katori 10 centimetres above the middle of a plate while a food pours into a heap.
setup.caption: 3. Pour the food slowly onto the plate from 10 centimetres up.

setup.art: A ruler standing next to a small heap of food on a plate, measuring its height in millimetres.
setup.caption: 4. Stand the ruler beside the heap and read its height in millimetres.

setup.art: A square map with mass along the bottom, heap height up the side, and ten labelled dots, three of them ringed together.
setup.caption: 5. Draw the map. Put one dot for each food. Ring the clumps.

flow.do: Line up the ten foods. Ask your child to guess which will be the heaviest in a katori and which the lightest. Ask which will make the tallest heap. Write the guesses and the reasons.
flow.say: We will measure two things about ten foods. First, how heavy one katori of each is. Second, how tall a heap each makes. Which will be heaviest? Which will make the tallest heap? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess first. Which food is heaviest in a katori? Which piles tallest? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think that food will be the heaviest, or make the tallest heap?
good: It is made of big grains.
Flour is light and fluffy.
Salt is a heavy crystal.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guesses. Any guess with a reason is a good start. Write your child's own words.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Katori Map. You guess before you measure.

flow.do: Put the empty katori on the scale and press zero. If your scale has no zero button, weigh the empty katori and subtract it later. Fill the katori with salt and level the top with a ruler. Weigh it and write the grams. Do the same for the other nine foods.
flow.say: Weigh one katori of each food. Fill it level every time. Write the grams in the table.
flow.kid: Fill the katori level. Weigh it. Write the grams. Do all ten foods.
flow.parent: Keep the food in the katori after weighing, to use for the heap in step four. If you have no scale at home, a kirana shop or a neighbour will often weigh the katoris. Without a scale, rank the ten katoris by holding two at a time, and use the ranks 1 to 10 instead of grams. One child with a parent: the child fills, levels and weighs, and the parent writes the table. Two to four children: one fills and levels, one weighs and one writes. Swap jobs after every food. Each child then draws their own map from the shared table. Typical masses of a steel katori of food are roughly 70 to 200 grams, but katoris differ, so trust your own numbers.

check.q: Why do you level the top of the katori for every food?
options: So the katori looks neat
So the food does not spill
So every food has the same volume, and only the food changes
check.why: In a fair test, only one thing changes. If one katori were heaped and another were half full, you would not know whether the food or the amount made the difference. Neatness and spilling are not the reason.

flow.context: In this step, you weigh one katori of each of the ten foods.

flow.do: Write the ten foods in a column, from the lightest to the heaviest. This is your ladder. Draw a line where you think the heavy foods begin. Ask a family member to draw their line on their own copy. Compare the two lines.
flow.say: Write the foods in order, lightest to heaviest. Draw a line where heavy foods begin. Ask someone else to draw theirs. Are the groups the same?
flow.kid: Make the ladder. Draw your line. Ask a friend to draw theirs.

ask.q: Which foods were in the same group whatever line was drawn?
good: The lightest and the heaviest.
The ones at the ends of the ladder.
The ones far from the lines.

flow.parent: People usually agree on the ends of the ladder and disagree in the middle. There is no right line. Do not decide who is right.
flow.context: In this step, you make the ladder and draw a cut-off line.

flow.do: Spread newspaper and put the plate on it. Hold the katori of food about 10 centimetres above the middle of the plate. Pour slowly into a heap. Stand the ruler beside the heap and read its height in millimetres. Pour the food back, and do it again. Do this for all ten foods.
flow.say: Pour each food slowly onto the plate from 10 centimetres up. Measure the height of the heap in millimetres. Do each food twice.
flow.kid: Pour the food into a heap. Measure the height. Do it twice.
flow.parent: Flours make dust, so pour slowly. Smooth, round seeds such as mustard usually make flatter heaps, and flours usually make taller ones, but write down what you get. If a heap slumps, measure the height after it settles. The heap can be 50 millimetres tall, so pouring from 10 centimetres keeps the katori clear of the heap. Tilt the katori slowly so the food falls in a thin stream. One child pours, one reads the ruler at eye level and one writes. Swap for the second pour. If two pours differ by more than 5 millimetres, pour a third time and average the two closest. Typical heaps are roughly 20 to 60 millimetres, but your numbers may differ. In damp or hot weather, salt, sugar and flours soak up water and form lumps. Keep each food in a closed jar until its turn and say in your notes if a food lumps.

check.q: Why do you pour every food from the same height?
options: So that the flour stays clean
So that the plate stays full
So that the way you pour does not change the heap
check.why: If you poured one food from high up and another from low down, the heaps would differ because of the pouring and not because of the food. Cleanliness and a full plate have nothing to do with it.

flow.context: In this step, you pour each food into a heap and measure its height.

flow.do: Draw two lines on the paper. Along the bottom, write mass in grams. Up the side, write height in millimetres. For each food, find its mass across and its average height up, and put a dot there. Write the food name by the dot. Then ring any dots that sit close together.
flow.say: Draw your map. Mass goes across and height goes up. Put a dot for each food. Which dots sit close together? Draw a ring round each clump.
flow.kid: Draw the map. One dot for each food. Ring the dots that sit together.

ask.q: What do you notice about the dots on your map?
good: Some dots are close together.
A few foods sit alone.
The flours are together.

flow.parent: You may see clumps such as flours together, smooth seeds together and salt and sugar together. You may not. Both are results. Poha or another food may sit far from the others, and that is also a result.
flow.context: In this step, you draw the map and look for clumps.

flow.do: Compare your ladder and your map. Ask your child to say or write three sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened. Ask where they would draw the groups now.
flow.say: Look at the ladder and at the map. Write three sentences. What did you think? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three sentences. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer says that the ladder had no clear gap, so the line was a choice, and that the map may have shown clumps or none. If the foods did not clump, that is also a finding: it means these two numbers do not split these foods. Let your child try first. Then read the Clumps and Gaps card together.
flow.context: In this step, you compare the ladder and the map and explain what you found.

experiments.title: Strict or Relaxed? Two ways to sort, two kinds of mistake
