experiments.question: When you sort a mix of two look-alike dals under a time limit, what happens to the mistakes if you are strict, and if you are relaxed?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. If you take only the pieces you are sure of, will you make fewer mistakes than if you take every piece that might be right? What kinds of mistake will each way make? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Each round uses the same mix of twenty toor dal and twenty chana dal. Each round lasts thirty seconds, with the same bowls on the same tray. Only the rule changes. In one round you take only the pieces you are sure of. In the other you take every piece that might be toor dal.
results_table: Chana dal in the toor bowl (wrongly let through)
Toor dal not in the bowl (wrongly kept back)

materials.item: 20 pieces of toor dal and 20 pieces of chana dal
a tray
2 small bowls
a clock or phone with a stopwatch
a pencil and the results table
a second person to count and to be the timekeeper

experiments.safety: Dry dal can be a choking risk for children under five. Do not eat the dal in this test. Wash your hands after. Pick up any dal that falls on the floor, so nobody slips.
experiments.record: For each round, write how many pieces are in the toor bowl. Then count carefully how many of those are chana dal. Work out how many toor dal pieces are not in the bowl.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you sort a mix of toor dal and chana dal twice, in thirty seconds each time. In one round you are strict and in the other you are relaxed. Then you count the two kinds of mistake.

setup.art: Twenty toor dal and twenty chana dal in two small heaps side by side on a tray, with a hand pointing at the small difference in size and shade.
setup.caption: 1. Look at both dals side by side. They look much alike.

setup.art: The two dals mixed together in one heap on the tray with two empty bowls beside it and a phone timer set to 30 seconds.
setup.caption: 2. Mix the dals into one heap. Set the timer for 30 seconds.

setup.art: A child moving pieces from the heap into the bowl marked toor while a grown-up watches the timer.
setup.caption: 3. Move pieces into the toor bowl until the time is up.

setup.art: A grown-up counting the pieces in the toor bowl and pointing out the chana dal that has crept in.
setup.caption: 4. Count the pieces in the bowl and find the chana dal that does not belong.

setup.art: A results table with two rows, strict and relaxed, and numbers written in the columns.
setup.caption: 5. Write the counts in the table for the strict round and the relaxed round.

flow.do: Show your child the two bowls and the mixed dals. Ask for a guess and a reason before anything is sorted. Write the guess at the top of the results table.
flow.say: We will sort toor dal from chana dal, in thirty seconds. In one round you take only pieces you are sure of. In the other round you take every piece that might be toor dal. Which round will make fewer mistakes? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess first. Which way makes fewer mistakes? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Why do you think that way will make fewer mistakes?
good: If I am careful I will be right more.
If I take everything I will miss nothing.
Each way will make a different kind of mistake.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start.
flow.context: This is the first step of Strict or Relaxed. You guess before you sort.

flow.do: A grown-up counts out 20 toor dal and 20 chana dal. Put them in two heaps side by side. Ask your child what is different about them. Then mix the two heaps into one on the tray.
flow.say: Look at the two dals side by side. What is different? What is alike? Now we mix them into one heap.
flow.kid: Look at both dals. How are they different? Now mix them up.

ask.q: What is different about the two dals?
good: One is a little bigger.
One is a deeper yellow.
They look almost the same.

flow.parent: Chana dal pieces are usually a little larger and a deeper yellow than toor dal, but brands differ. They look much alike, and that is the point. If yours look very different, use two dals that look more alike, such as toor dal and split moong dal with its skin removed. If your child makes no mistakes in either round, that is a real result. Make the task harder. Use 15 seconds instead of 30, or sort from arm's length, or use the more alike pair. Mistakes then appear, because hurry and doubt cause them. One child with a parent: the parent keeps time and counts. Two to four children: each child sorts their own 20 and 20 on a tray, while another child times and a third counts. Rotate the jobs and give each sorter a row in the table. Compare the rows.
flow.context: In this step, you meet the two dals and mix them into one heap.

flow.do: Set the timer for 30 seconds. Say go. Your child moves into the toor bowl only the pieces they are very sure are toor dal. Stop when the timer ends. Then count the pieces in the bowl, and count carefully how many of them are chana dal.
flow.say: Strict round. Take only the pieces you are very sure are toor dal. You have thirty seconds. Ready, go. Now stop, and count.
flow.kid: Strict round. Take only pieces you are sure of. Thirty seconds. Go.
flow.parent: Count slowly with no time limit, because the aim now is to find every mistake. Toor dal not in the bowl is 20 minus the toor dal that is in the bowl. A strict round often leaves many good pieces behind and has almost no chana dal in the bowl.

check.q: In a strict round, the toor bowl had 9 pieces and all were toor dal. 11 toor dal were left in the heap. What kind of mistake were the 11?
options: No mistake at all
Wrongly let through
Wrongly kept back
check.why: The 11 toor dal pieces belonged in the toor bowl but were held back. That is a wrongly kept back mistake. Wrongly let through would be a chana dal piece in the bowl, and there was none.

flow.context: In this step, you do the strict round and count your mistakes.

flow.do: Mix all 40 pieces into one heap again. Set the timer for 30 seconds. This time, your child moves into the toor bowl every piece that might be toor dal. Stop when the timer ends. Count the pieces in the bowl, and the chana dal among them.
flow.say: Relaxed round. Take every piece that might be toor dal. You have thirty seconds. Ready, go. Now stop, and count.
flow.kid: Relaxed round. Take every piece that might be toor dal. Thirty seconds. Go.
flow.parent: A relaxed round often has more chana dal in the bowl and fewer toor dal left behind. If you did not get this pattern, write down what you saw. Some people are careful whatever the rule.

check.q: In a relaxed round, the toor bowl had 30 pieces and 11 of them were chana dal. What kind of mistake were those 11?
options: Wrongly let through
No mistake at all
Wrongly kept back
check.why: The 11 chana dal pieces do not belong in the toor bowl, but they were let in. That is a wrongly let through mistake. Wrongly kept back would be toor dal still in the heap.

flow.context: In this step, you do the relaxed round and count your mistakes.

flow.do: Fill in the table for both rounds. Add the two kinds of mistake for each round. Ask your child to say or write three sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Write the counts in your table. Add up the mistakes for each round. Write three sentences. What did you think? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Fill in the table. Say or write three sentences. What I think. What I saw. Why.

ask.q: What happened to the two kinds of mistake when you changed from strict to relaxed?
good: One kind went down and the other went up.
The mistakes just swapped.
Neither round was perfect.

flow.parent: A good reason says that the two groups look alike, so no rule can be right every time. Moving from strict to relaxed swaps one kind of mistake for the other. Let your child say it first. Then read the Trade-off card together. The second round is easier because the pieces are now familiar. To be fair, let the next sorter, or the next day, do the relaxed round first and see if the pattern holds.
flow.context: In this step, you total the mistakes and explain what you found.

experiments.title: Soft or Hard? Five voters, one ladder
experiments.question: Do people agree on where soft ends and hard begins? Which things do all voters put in the same group, and which split the vote? Does a test make the votes agree more?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Out of ten things, how many will all five voters put in the same group? Which things will split the vote? Will a test with a fingernail make the votes agree more? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every voter touches every thing in the same way. Voters write their answers secretly, so nobody copies. The things stay in the same order on the tray. Only the voter changes, so any difference in the votes comes from the people and not from the things.
results_table: Round 1: voters who said hard (0 to 5, or out of your number of voters)
Round 2: voters who found no dent (0 to 5, or out of your number of voters)

materials.item: 10 things: a cotton wool ball, a kitchen sponge, a folded towel, a lump of stiff atta dough, not sticky, or modelling clay, a rubber eraser, an empty plastic bottle with the cap on, a candle, a wooden spoon, a steel katori and a ceramic cup
5 voters, such as parents, brothers, sisters or neighbours, and your child can be one. With fewer people, 3 voters is enough
5 slips of paper with ten lines on each, and 5 pencils
a tray to hold the ten things in a row
a clock or phone with a stopwatch
the results table on a sheet of paper

experiments.safety: Fingernails press only a gentle push. Do not use a knife or a sharp thing. Use an unlit candle, and keep it away from flames and matches.
experiments.record: For each thing, write how many voters said hard in round 1 and how many found no dent in round 2. Then put the ten things in order, from the most votes for hard to the fewest. Also count how many things all the voters agreed on in each round.
experiments.context: In this experiment, five voters decide whether ten things are soft or hard, first by their own feeling and then by a fingernail test. You find which things split the vote.

setup.art: Ten household things laid in a row on a tray: cotton wool, a sponge, a towel, dough, an eraser, a plastic bottle, a candle, a wooden spoon, a steel katori and a ceramic cup.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the ten things in a row. Give each voter a slip with ten lines.

setup.art: A voter pressing a rubber eraser between a finger and thumb and writing an H or an S on a slip held out of sight.
setup.caption: 2. Round 1: each voter presses each thing and writes hard or soft on the slip, in secret.

setup.art: A fingernail pressing into a candle for three seconds, with a small dent showing, and a timer in the background.
setup.caption: 3. Round 2: press a fingernail into each thing for three seconds. Does it leave a dent?

setup.art: A results table with ten rows and two columns of vote counts, with a line drawn across the table.
setup.caption: 4. Count the votes for each thing. Put the things in order, and draw your line.

flow.do: Show your child the ten things and the voters. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write the guess at the top of the results table.
flow.say: We have ten things and five voters. Each voter decides if each thing is soft or hard. Will they all agree? Which things might split the vote? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess first. Will all the voters agree? Which things might split the vote?

ask.q: Which thing do you think will split the vote?
good: The eraser.
The candle.
The plastic bottle.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start.
flow.context: This is the first step of Soft or Hard. You guess before you vote.

flow.do: Lay the ten things in a row on the tray. Give each voter a slip with ten lines, one for each thing, and a pencil. Explain that each voter will write H for hard or S for soft, and must not show the others.
flow.say: Here are the ten things. Each of you will write H for hard or S for soft on your own slip. Do not show anyone. Do not copy.
flow.kid: Lay out the ten things. Give each voter a slip.
flow.context: In this step, you set out the things and explain the voting.
flow.parent: One child with a parent: use 3 voters if you can, such as the child, the parent and one other person, and divide each count by the number of voters. Two to four children: each child votes, with a parent as the last voter and the tray keeper. Make a copy of the slips for every voter. Several slips can be filled in at the same time.

flow.do: Round 1. Each voter presses each thing once with a finger and thumb, and writes H or S on the slip. Take turns, so the voters do not see each other's slips. Then collect the slips.
flow.say: Round one. Press each thing once with a finger and thumb. Write H for hard or S for soft. Keep your slip secret.
flow.kid: Press each thing. Write H or S. Keep it secret.
flow.parent: Use the word hard for a thing that does not squash when pressed. Do not say more. Let each voter use their own idea of hard. Collect the slips before anybody talks.
flow.context: In this step, you hold round 1 of the vote.

flow.do: Round 2. Each voter presses a fingernail into each thing with a steady push for three seconds. They write D if the nail sinks in and leaves a hollow they can see, and N if it does not. Keep the slips secret. Then collect them.
flow.say: Round two. Press your fingernail into each thing for three seconds. Write D if it leaves a dent. Write N if it does not.
flow.kid: Press a fingernail into each thing. Write D or N. Keep it secret.
flow.parent: Press with a steady push. About three seconds is enough. A few things, such as the candle and the eraser, may still split the vote. Write what you see. Use the flat end of a pencil if a child's nails are very short. On a hot day the candle and dough are softer and may get more D votes, so write the weather in your notes.

check.q: Round 2 gives every voter the same test. What do you expect to happen to the votes?
options: The votes will not change at all
The voters will agree more, because the test is clearer than a feeling
The voters will agree less
check.why: A test that everyone does in the same way takes away some of the guessing, so the votes usually agree more. Some things, such as an eraser or a plastic bottle, may still split the vote. That tells you the thing is really in the middle.

flow.context: In this step, you hold round 2 of the vote, with a fingernail test.

flow.do: Count the votes for each thing and write them in the table. Put the things in order, from the most votes for hard to the fewest. Draw a line where soft ends and hard begins. Mark the things that split the vote. Count how many things all voters agreed on in each round.
flow.say: Count the votes. Put the things in order. Draw your line. Which things split the vote?
flow.kid: Count the votes. Put the things in order. Mark the ones that split.

ask.q: Which things did every voter agree on, in both rounds?
good: The cotton wool and the sponge.
The steel katori and the ceramic cup.
The things at the two ends of the ladder.

flow.context: In this step, you count the votes and make a ladder from them.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened. Ask which round had more agreement.
flow.say: Write three sentences. What did you think? What did you see? Why do you think it happened? Which round had more agreement?
flow.kid: Say or write three sentences. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good reason says that the things in the middle of the ladder split the vote. A clear test makes people agree more, but it cannot remove the middle. Let your child try first. Then read the Moving the Cut-off card together.
flow.context: In this step, you explain what you found.

activities.title: Plastic Code Hunt: the number in the triangle

materials.item: 8 to 10 plastic things from around the house that show a triangle of arrows with a number, such as a water bottle, a curd cup, a tiffin box, a shampoo bottle and a bottle cap
a magnifying glass, or your phone camera zoomed in on the base of each thing
a sheet of paper and a pencil
8 to 10 small sticky notes or slips of paper

activities.safety: Wash the plastic things before you handle them. Do not cut or break the plastic. Use only clean, empty food and drink containers. Never use anything that held bleach, toilet cleaner, pesticide or other chemicals. Keep small caps away from little children.

schedule.what: Find the codes. Sort by code. Compare what each group is used for and how it feels.

activities.record: A table with each thing, the number in its triangle, what it is used for, and whether it is clear, floppy or stiff.
activities.context: In this activity, you look at the number in the triangle on plastic things and sort them by it. You find out whether things with the same number are alike.

setup.art: The bottom of a water bottle showing a triangle of three arrows with the number 1 inside it, and a magnifying glass above it.
setup.caption: 1. Turn each plastic thing over. Find the triangle and the number.

setup.art: Plastic things in rows on a table, one row for each number, with a slip of paper above each row giving the number.
setup.caption: 2. Sort the things into rows by their number.

setup.art: A child squeezing a plastic bottle and a tiffin box lid, comparing how they feel.
setup.caption: 3. Squeeze, bend and look at each thing. Write down what each group is like.

flow.do: Collect 8 to 10 plastic things from the kitchen and bathroom. Before you start, guess how many things will show a number. Turn each one over and look for a triangle of arrows with a number. The marks are small, so tilt each thing under a light. Write down the number, and the thing it is on. If a thing has no mark, write none.
flow.say: Look at the bottom of each plastic thing. Find the triangle with a number in it. Write the number and the thing.
flow.kid: Find the number in the triangle on each thing. Write it down.

ask.q: What do you think the number in the triangle tells us?
good: How strong the plastic is.
What kind of plastic it is.
How many times it can be used.

flow.parent: Many things in India carry no mark at all. If you find fewer than four with a code, borrow things from a neighbour or look at bigger containers, such as a bucket or an oil can. Do not tell your child yet what the number means. Let them guess. Some packs in India show only letters such as PET, HDPE or PP, or no mark at all. Count those too. None is a result. Carry bags, pouches and chips packets often have no number. One child with a parent: the parent holds the list. Two to four children: each child hunts in one room, such as the kitchen, the bathroom or the store room, and finds at least three things.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Plastic Code Hunt. You find the codes.

flow.do: Lay the things in rows, one row for each number. Under each row, write what the things are used for. Ask your child to squeeze and bend each thing gently, and to say if it is clear, floppy or stiff.
flow.say: Put the things with the same number in a row. What are they used for? Squeeze them. How do they feel?
flow.kid: Make a row for each number. Squeeze each thing. Write how it feels.
flow.parent: You will usually see that bottles share one or two numbers, and tiffin boxes and curd cups share another. Numbers 1, 2 and 5 are the commonest in homes. A 7 means other.

check.q: Two things have the number 5 in the triangle. What can you say about them?
options: They are exactly the same shape
They are made of the same family of plastic
They can be recycled in any town
check.why: The number names the family of plastic. Two things with a 5 are made of the same family. They can have very different shapes. The code does not say whether your town can recycle them.

flow.context: In this step, you sort the things by code and compare what each group is like.

flow.do: Read what the numbers mean: 1 is PET, often clear drink bottles. 2 is HDPE, often milk cans and shampoo bottles. 5 is polypropylene, often tiffin boxes and curd cups. 7 is other. Also, 3 is PVC, 4 is LDPE like milk pouches and carry bags, and 6 is polystyrene like some cups. Check each row against your list.
flow.say: The number names the family of plastic. Check your rows. Does each row hold what the number says?
flow.kid: Check your rows against the list. Which row was the biggest?

ask.q: Why is there a number 7, for other?
good: Some plastics do not fit the first six.
It is for mixtures.
It is the tricky middle.

flow.parent: Number 7 is a box for everything that does not fit the first six. It is the tricky middle from the earlier unit on sorting. A thing marked 7 may hold many different plastics, so recycling plants often cannot sort it.
flow.context: In this step, you check your rows against what the numbers mean.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Write three sentences. What did you think? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three sentences. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good reason says that things with the same number are alike in what they are made of, and often in how they feel and what they are used for. The code is a sort by one question, what family of plastic, so it hides other differences, such as colour and shape.
flow.context: In this step, you explain what you found.

activities.title: Lumpers and Splitters: sort the spice shelf at three levels

materials.item: 12 kitchen spices in small katoris or saucers, such as mustard, cumin, fennel, coriander seeds, turmeric, chilli powder, coriander powder, dry curry leaves, a bay leaf, a cinnamon stick, cardamom and cloves. Swap in black pepper, fenugreek, ajwain, sesame or star anise for any you lack
a big sheet of paper and a pencil
a helper who will look for one spice

activities.safety: Do not eat or sniff the spices closely. Keep chilli powder away from your eyes, and do not rub your eyes. Leave out any spice that your child is allergic to. Wash your hands after. Keep cloves, cardamom and other small spices away from little children's mouths, ears and noses.

schedule.what: Sort twelve spices into 2 groups, then 4, then 8. Draw the tree. Test which level is fastest for a job.

activities.record: A tree drawing with the 12 spices, the groups at each level, and a count of how many things a helper looked at to find one spice at each level.
activities.context: In this activity, you sort twelve spices at three levels, from a few big groups to many small ones. You test which level suits which job.

setup.art: Twelve small katoris of spices laid in a row on a table, with two big circles of paper labelled with two group names.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the twelve spices. Sort them into two big groups.

setup.art: The same twelve spices now in four smaller groups, with each group in its own circle.
setup.caption: 2. Split each big group in two, to make four groups.

setup.art: A tree diagram on paper with the two big groups at the top, four medium groups below and eight small groups at the bottom.
setup.caption: 3. Split again, to make eight groups. Draw the tree.

flow.do: Lay out the twelve spices. Ask your child to sort them into two groups using any rule they like, and to say the rule. Then split each group in two to make four groups. Write the rule for each split.
flow.say: Sort the spices into two groups. What is your rule? Now split each group in two. What are the new rules?
flow.kid: Sort the spices into two groups. Then split each group again.

ask.q: What rule did you use for the first two groups?
good: Seeds and not seeds.
Powder and not powder.
Hot and not hot.

flow.parent: Any rule is fine, as long as the child can say it. Examples are seeds and powders, strong smell and mild smell, or things that go in the pan first and things that go in last. One child with a parent: the parent is the helper. Two to four children: one sorts, one is the helper who looks for the spice, one counts, and you rotate. Or each child sorts their own spices and then compares the trees.
flow.context: This is the first step of Lumpers and Splitters. You sort at two levels.

flow.do: Split each of the four groups again to make about eight groups. Some groups may hold only one spice. Draw a tree on the big sheet. Put the two first groups at the top and the eight small groups at the bottom.
flow.say: Split the groups again, until you have about eight. Draw a tree. Two groups at the top, eight at the bottom.
flow.kid: Split again to make eight groups. Draw the tree.
flow.parent: Do not worry if the groups are uneven. The tree is a way to show the levels. It is fine if some groups have one spice.

check.q: A shelf with 2 big groups, each split into 2, and each of those split into 2 has how many small groups?
check.why: Two groups, each split in two, make four. Four groups, each split in two, make eight. That is 2 times 2 times 2, which is 8. Six would be a count that adds instead of multiplying.

flow.context: In this step, you split to a third level and draw the tree.

flow.do: A helper closes their eyes. You secretly pick one spice. The helper asks yes or no questions to find it, using only the groups at one level. Count each group the helper names and each spice the helper looks at. Hide a different spice each time. Find two spices at each level and average the counts. Try it at the two-group level, the four-group level and the eight-group level.
flow.say: Pick a secret spice. Your helper uses the groups to find it. Count how many things they check. Try it at each level.
flow.kid: Pick a secret spice. Let a helper find it with the groups. Count the checks.

ask.q: At which level did the helper find the spice with the fewest checks?
good: The finest level, with eight groups.
The level with the smallest groups.
The coarse level took the most checks.

flow.parent: At the coarse level, the helper must still look through six spices. At the fine level, only one or two. But making and remembering eight groups takes more effort than two. Expect the middle level to need the fewest looks. Two groups leave many spices in each group, and eight groups leave many groups to check. Two finds per level are few, so repeat if the numbers look odd. That is also a result.
flow.context: In this step, you test how well each level helps to find a spice.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened. Ask which level they would use to put the spices away.
flow.say: Write three sentences. What did you think? What did you see? Why do you think it happened? Which level would you choose?
flow.kid: Say or write three sentences. Which level would you use, and why?
flow.parent: A good answer says that the right level depends on the job. A coarse level is quick to set up, and a fine level is quick to search. A job that needs only to know seeds from powders can lump. A job that needs to find cumin in the dark must split.
flow.context: In this step, you explain what you found and choose a level.

activities.title: Star Map: be Hertzsprung and Russell

materials.item: a sheet of squared paper, or plain paper with a 5 by 5 grid drawn on it
a pencil and 5 coloured pencils: red, orange, yellow, white or grey, and blue
the list of 16 stars in the steps

schedule.what: Plot sixteen stars by colour and brightness. Ring the clumps. Name the families.

activities.record: A star map with sixteen dots, rings round the clumps, and a name for each clump.
activities.context: In this activity, you place sixteen real stars on a map by colour and brightness, as Hertzsprung and Russell did. You look for families of stars.

setup.art: A 5 by 5 grid on paper with colour across the bottom from red on the left to blue on the right, and brightness up the side from very faint to very bright.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the grid. Colour goes across and brightness goes up.

setup.art: Sixteen coloured dots on the grid, spread in a band from bottom left to top right, with a few dots above and one below the band.
setup.caption: 2. Put a dot for each star. Use the colour of the star for the dot.

setup.art: The same grid with three rings drawn round the band, the dots above it and the dot below it.
setup.caption: 3. Ring the clumps. Name each family.

flow.do: Draw a grid of 5 squares across and 5 up. Make each square about 3 centimetres wide. Before you plot, guess if the dots will spread evenly or gather. Across the bottom, write colour: 1 red, 2 orange, 3 yellow, 4 white, 5 blue-white. Up the side, write brightness: 1 very faint, 2 faint, 3 like the Sun, 4 bright, 5 very bright. The steps are rough.
flow.say: Draw a grid, five by five. Colour goes along the bottom, from red to blue. Brightness goes up the side, from very faint to very bright.
flow.kid: Draw the grid. Colour goes across. Brightness goes up.
flow.parent: This is a simplified version of a real star map. The steps are rough ranks, and the star values are rounded. Stars differ so much in brightness that astronomers use a special scale, but ranks show the same families.
flow.context: This is the first step of Star Map. You draw the grid.

flow.do: Plot these stars, as colour step then brightness step. Proxima Centauri, 1 and 1. Barnard's Star, 1 and 1. 61 Cygni A, 2 and 2. Epsilon Eridani, 2 and 2. The Sun, 3 and 3. Alpha Centauri A, 3 and 3. Sirius A, 4 and 4. Vega, 4 and 4. Altair, 4 and 4. Spica, 5 and 5. Rigel, 5 and 5. Arcturus, 2 and 4. Aldebaran, 2 and 4. Betelgeuse, 1 and 5. Antares, 1 and 5. Sirius B, 4 and 2.
flow.say: Plot all sixteen stars. Colour step goes across and brightness step goes up. Put dots side by side if two stars share a square.
flow.kid: Plot the sixteen stars. Colour across, brightness up.
flow.parent: Stars that share a square can be drawn as two dots side by side. Colour the dot to match the star's colour. Betelgeuse and Antares are red, Arcturus and Aldebaran are orange, the Sun is yellow, Sirius is white, and Rigel and Spica are blue-white. Some squares hold two or three stars. Draw the dots side by side in the square. One child with a parent: the parent reads the list and the child plots. Two to four children: share one big sheet and let each child plot four stars, then ring the clumps together.
flow.context: In this step, you plot sixteen real stars on your map.

flow.do: Look at the map. Do the dots spread evenly, or do they gather? Draw a ring round the long band of dots from bottom left to top right. Draw a ring round the dots above the band, and a ring round the dot below the band.
flow.say: Look at the map. Where do the dots gather? Draw a ring round each clump. Is there a band? What sits above it? What sits below it?
flow.kid: Ring the clumps. Find the band, the dots above and the dot below.

ask.q: What would you call the stars above the band, and the star below it?
good: Bright cool giants above, and a small hot faint star below.
Giants and a dwarf.
Big stars and a small one.

flow.parent: The long band is called the main sequence, and the Sun sits on it. The bright orange and red stars above the band are giants. The single dot below is a white dwarf, Sirius B. Rigel is really a blue supergiant, but at these rough steps it lands at the top corner of the band.

check.q: The dots do not fill the map evenly. They form a band, and there are empty areas. What does this show?
options: All stars are the same
The stars come in families, and not all combinations of colour and brightness exist
The stars are in the wrong places
check.why: If stars could have any colour and any brightness, the dots would fill the map. They gather in a band, with a few above and below. So stars come in families. Wrong places and all stars being the same would not make a pattern.

flow.context: In this step, you find the families of stars on your map.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened. Ask what the map shows that a plain list of stars did not.
flow.say: Write three sentences. What did you think? What did you see? Why do you think it happened? What did the map show that a list did not?
flow.kid: Say or write three sentences. What did the map show that a list could not?
flow.parent: A good answer says that a list of names and numbers hides the pattern, and a map makes it clear: the band, the giants and the white dwarf. Hertzsprung and Russell found families of stars in this way, before anybody knew why they were there.
flow.context: In this step, you explain what you found.

activities.title: Shelf Detective: how a kirana store sorts its goods

materials.item: a kirana store, a supermarket aisle or your own kitchen cupboards. The kitchen is enough if no shop is near
a notebook and a pencil
a grown-up to come with you

activities.safety: Go with a grown-up. Do not touch things you do not plan to buy. Ask the shopkeeper before you take notes or photographs. Stay beside your grown-up near roads and in crowded shops. Go at a quiet hour.

schedule.what: Visit a store or a cupboard. Find the groups, the levels and the things that could be in two places.

activities.record: A list of the shelf groups, the rule for each, the number of levels, and two things that could go in two places.
activities.context: In this activity, you look at how a real store sorts its goods. You find the rules, the levels and the tricky things that could go in two places.

setup.art: A kirana store shelf with groups labelled rice, dals, oils and spices, and a child writing the names in a notebook.
setup.caption: 1. Walk along the shelves. Write down each group.

setup.art: A page in a notebook with a tree of groups: grocery at the top, then dals and spices, then toor dal and moong dal.
setup.caption: 2. Draw the levels as a tree.

flow.do: Visit a kirana store, a supermarket aisle or the kitchen cupboards. Many kirana shops keep goods behind the counter, so ask the shopkeeper to point out the groups. Ask your child to walk along the shelves and write down each group of goods. Ask what rule the shop uses for each group.
flow.say: Walk along the shelves with a grown-up. Write down each group. What rule does the shop use for it?
flow.kid: Walk along the shelves. Write down each group and its rule.

ask.q: What rule does the shop use to put things together?
good: By what they are, like dals or oils.
By how they are used, like things for cooking.
By brand.

flow.parent: Kirana stores often sort by use, such as things for the morning, things for the kitchen and things for cleaning. They also sort by size and by how often things sell. Ask the shopkeeper why. Mid-morning is usually quiet. Buying one small thing is a kind thanks. Two to four children: each takes a different shelf or cupboard, then compare trees.
flow.context: This is the first step of Shelf Detective. You find the groups.

flow.do: Find a group that has smaller groups inside it, such as dals with toor dal and moong dal inside. Draw a tree of these levels. Pick one item, such as turmeric, and count the groups you check before you find it. Count the levels. Then look for one thing that could go in two places, and say where you would put it.
flow.say: Find a group with smaller groups inside. Draw the tree. How many levels? Find a thing that could go in two places.
flow.kid: Draw the levels as a tree. Find a thing that fits two groups.
flow.parent: Good examples are salt, turmeric, tea, jaggery and papad. Ask the shopkeeper why the shop put the thing there.

check.q: A shop keeps salt with the spices, but another shop keeps it with the staples next to rice. What does this show?
options: There are several useful ways to sort the same thing, and the rule is the shop's choice
Salt is a spice by nature
One shop is wrong
check.why: Neither shop is wrong. Each uses a rule that suits its customers. The rule is a choice, so the same thing can land in different groups in different shops.

flow.context: In this step, you draw the levels and find a thing that could go in two places.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think the shop sorts that way. Ask which level the shop uses the most.
flow.say: Write three sentences. What did you think? What did you see? Why does the shop sort that way?
flow.kid: Say or write three sentences. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good reason says that the shop sorts to help the customer find things quickly, and the rule fits the job. Most shops use two or three levels: aisle, shelf group and brand.
flow.context: In this step, you explain what you found.

projects.title: Predict Where It Lands: add new foods to the Katori Map

materials.item: your Katori Map from the experiment, and the same katori, plate, scale and ruler
about one katori each of six new dry foods, such as besan, cornflour, rolled oats, sabudana, masoor dal and sesame seeds. Buy small packets only of those you lack, or borrow a katori from a neighbour
a pencil and a different coloured pen for the predictions
newspaper to spread under the plate

projects.safety: Do not eat the foods in this test. Flour dust can make you sneeze, so pour slowly and keep your face away. Leave out any food that your child is allergic to. Wash your hands after. Keep small grains and seeds away from little children's mouths and noses.

schedule.what: Predict where six new foods will land on the map. Measure them. Compare.

projects.record: The Katori Map with a cross for each prediction and a dot for each real result, and a count of how many predictions were close.
projects.context: In this project, you use your Katori Map to predict where new foods will land. Then you measure them and see how good the map is at predicting.

setup.art: A Katori Map with six pencil crosses in a different colour, each cross labelled with the name of a new food.
setup.caption: 1. Predict where each new food will land. Mark it with a cross.

setup.art: A child weighing a katori of besan on a kitchen scale and pouring a second katori of it into a heap.
setup.caption: 2. Weigh each new food and measure its heap, exactly as before.

setup.art: The Katori Map with crosses and dots joined by short lines, showing how far each prediction was from the real result.
setup.caption: 3. Plot the real results. Draw a line from each cross to its dot.

flow.do: Take out your Katori Map. Look at the six new foods. For each one, decide which clump it will join, and mark a cross where you think its dot will be. Write the reason in one short line.
flow.say: Look at your map and the six new foods. Where will each one land? Mark a cross. Write why.
flow.kid: Mark a cross for each new food. Write why you put it there.

ask.q: Why do you think that food will land there?
good: It is a flour, so it should be with the flours.
It looks like the rice.
It is light and flaky, like poha.

flow.parent: Do not correct the predictions. Any prediction with a reason is a good start. A prediction that turns out wrong teaches more than one that turns out right.
flow.context: This is the first step of Predict Where It Lands. You predict before you measure.

flow.do: Weigh one katori of each new food, filled level. Pour each into a heap from 10 centimetres up, twice, and measure the heights in millimetres. Write the mass and the average height for each food.
flow.say: Measure the six new foods just as before. Weigh a katori of each. Pour two heaps and measure them. Write the numbers.
flow.kid: Weigh and pour each new food, just as before. Write the numbers.
flow.parent: Use the same katori, the same plate, the same height for pouring and the same ruler. Flours make dust, so pour slowly. Short of time? Do four foods, or finish the rest in a second sitting. Two to four children: each child takes two or three foods and weighs, pours and measures them. One child with a parent: the parent writes and holds the ruler. Keep foods in closed jars in damp weather, and say if one lumps.

check.q: Why must you measure the new foods in exactly the same way as the first ten?
options: So the map looks neat
So the new foods taste the same
So the new dots can be compared fairly with the old ones
check.why: A map only makes sense if every dot is measured in the same way. If the new foods were poured from higher up, their heaps would differ for a reason that has nothing to do with the food.

flow.context: In this step, you measure the six new foods.

flow.do: Plot the real results on the map as dots. Draw a short line from each cross to its dot. Measure each line with a ruler in millimetres. Count how many predictions landed in the right clump.
flow.say: Plot the real dots. Draw a line from each cross to its dot. Measure the lines. Which prediction was closest?
flow.kid: Plot the real dots. Join each cross to its dot. Measure the lines.

ask.q: Which food surprised you most, and why?
good: Sabudana was heavier than I thought.
Oats made a flatter heap.
Besan landed with the other flours.

flow.context: In this step, you plot the real results and see how close your predictions were.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened. Ask what the map can and cannot predict.
flow.say: Write three sentences. What did you think? What did you see? Why do you think it happened? What can the map predict?
flow.kid: Say or write three sentences. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer says that the map predicts well when a new food is like the others in what matters for the two numbers, such as being a fine flour. It predicts badly when a new food has a shape or stickiness that the old foods did not have. An outlier teaches the most.
flow.context: In this step, you explain how good your map was at predicting.

challenges.title: The Slot Sorter: separate toor dal from chana dal with a gap
challenges.problem: You have a mix of 20 toor dal and 20 chana dal. Build a sorter with a slot that lets toor dal fall through into a bowl, while chana dal rolls on past. Make as few mistakes, of both kinds, as you can.
challenges.safety: Dry dal can be a choking risk for children under five. Do not eat the dal in this test. Pick up any dal that rolls onto the floor, so nobody slips. Wash your hands after.
constraints: Use only kitchen things and stationery, such as rulers, pencils, books and a tray.
Every test uses all 40 pieces, sent down once.
After every test, count both kinds of mistake: chana dal in the toor bowl, and toor dal that rolled past.
You may change only one thing at a time.
materials: 2 straight rulers, or 2 pencils or chopsticks of the same kind
a few books to prop one end of the rails
general: Two rulers lying side by side on a slope, with a narrow gap between them. Small pieces fall into the gap, and big pieces roll on.
A sieve, such as a tea strainer or a colander, whose holes are between the sizes of the two dals.
A tray with holes made by a pencil or a paper punch in a sheet of card.
creative: A slot that is narrow at the top and wider at the bottom, so that pieces fall through at the place that suits their width.
Two sorters one after the other, the first by size and the second by colour, picked by a second person.
A slope with a bump or a lip that makes the heavier or rounder pieces bounce further.
challenges.your_turn: Sketch your sorter. Measure the width of five pieces of each dal with a ruler, and choose a first gap. Build it and test it. Count both kinds of mistake. Change the gap, and test again. Which gap gave the fewest mistakes? Why can no gap give none?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about a sorter with an adjustable cut-off. You build a slot sorter, count both kinds of mistake, and move the cut-off to see what happens.

setup.art: Two rulers lying side by side on a slope made from books, with a small gap between them and a bowl under the gap.
setup.caption: 1. Lay two rulers on a slope with a small gap between them. Put a bowl under the gap.

setup.art: A child sending a small heap of dal down the rails, with small pieces falling through the gap and big pieces rolling to a bowl at the bottom.
setup.caption: 2. Send the dal down. Small pieces fall through. Big pieces roll on.

setup.art: A table with two bowls and a count of mistakes written beside each bowl.
setup.caption: 3. Count both kinds of mistake. Change the gap and test again.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Ask your child to measure the width of five pieces of each dal and write the numbers. Then ask them to sketch the sorter and choose a first gap.
flow.say: You have a mix of two dals. Measure five pieces of each. Which gap will let toor dal through but not chana dal? Draw your sorter.
flow.kid: Measure five pieces of each dal. Draw a sorter. Choose a gap.

ask.q: What gap would you choose, and why?
good: A gap just wider than the biggest toor dal.
A gap between the two sizes.
A gap in the middle of the numbers I measured.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Slot Sorter challenge. You plan before you build.

flow.do: Build the sorter. Prop one end of the rulers on books, so they slope. Set the gap and put a bowl below it. Send all 40 pieces down once. Count the chana dal in the toor bowl and the toor dal that rolled past.
flow.say: Build your sorter and send all forty pieces down once. Count the chana dal that fell through and the toor dal that rolled past.
flow.kid: Build the sorter. Send all 40 pieces down. Count both mistakes.
flow.parent: Pieces may stick or bounce. Tap the rulers gently if pieces stall. Dal pieces are not all the same size, so expect some mistakes. Write the numbers down. They are the ones to beat. If pieces bounce across the gap, make the slope gentler or pour a few at a time. Tape the ends of the rulers so the gap stays fixed. One child pours, and another counts.
flow.context: In this step, you build your sorter and test it.

flow.do: Change one thing only, such as the gap, the slope or the way you pour. Test again with all 40 pieces. Count both kinds of mistake. Try a third setting if you have time.
flow.say: Change one thing, such as the gap. Test again. Count both kinds of mistake. Which setting gave the fewest?
flow.kid: Change only the gap. Test again. Count both mistakes.
flow.parent: Common changes are the gap width, the slope of the rails and the pouring speed. Keep every other thing the same.

check.q: You made the gap wider. Fewer toor dal rolled past, but more chana dal fell through. What does this show?
options: The sorter is broken
Chana dal is lighter than toor dal
Moving the cut-off swapped one kind of mistake for the other
check.why: When two groups overlap in size, a wider gap lets in more of the big ones, and a narrower gap holds back more of the small ones. The mistakes have been swapped. A broken sorter would not give a pattern like this.

flow.context: In this step, you move the cut-off and test again.

flow.do: Compare your tests. Read the usual solutions and the creative ideas together. Ask your child why no gap gave zero mistakes, and what a second number might add.
flow.say: Which gap made the fewest mistakes? Why could no gap make none? Read the other ideas. What second number would help?
flow.kid: Which gap was best? Why no zero? Read the other ideas.

flow.parent: A good answer says that some pieces of the two dals overlap in size, so a gap cannot split them. A second number, such as colour, may separate them. This is what the rice mill in the story discovered.

opts: A number you choose to split a ladder into two groups
A gap that nature puts in a ladder
quiz.why: A cut-off is chosen by the person who sorts. It is not found in the things. Another person can choose another cut-off and make other groups.

quiz.p: When a cut-off moves, which things change group?
opts: Only the things at the ends
Only the things close to the cut-off
quiz.why: Things far from the cut-off stay in the same group whatever sensible cut-off you pick. Only the borderline ones move.

quiz.p: What can a map of two numbers show that a ladder of one number cannot?
quiz.why: A ladder puts things in a line, so it can show order. A map spreads things across two directions, so dots can gather into clumps and leave gaps.

quiz.p: A map of ten foods shows two clumps with a gap. A map of the same foods by two other numbers shows no gap. What does this tell you?
opts: One of the maps is wrong
The gap belonged to the first pair of numbers
quiz.why: A gap is a fact about the numbers plotted as well as about the things. A different pair of numbers can fill it in. Neither map is wrong.

quiz.p: A strict sorter takes only the pieces she is sure of. Which kind of mistake does she make more of?
quiz.why: A strict sorter holds back all the pieces she is not sure of, so many good ones are left behind. She lets in few wrong ones.

quiz.p: Two groups of seeds overlap in size. Why can no cut-off on size sort them without mistakes?
opts: Some seeds in one group are the same size as some in the other
quiz.why: If the sizes overlap, any cut-off puts some seeds on the wrong side. Only a second measurement, such as weight or colour, can help.

quiz.p: One shop sorts its spices into seeds and powders. Another shop sorts them into mustard, cumin, fennel and so on. What is the second shop doing?
quiz.why: A shop that makes many small groups is splitting. A shop that makes a few big groups is lumping. Both can be useful.

quiz.p: On a star map, where do most stars lie?
opts: In a long band called the main sequence
quiz.why: Stars gather in a long band, with a few giants above and a few white dwarfs below. That pattern is what showed that stars come in families.

quiz.p: The number 7 in the triangle on plastic means other, a box for plastics that do not fit the first six.
quiz.why: True. The codes 1 to 6 name particular families of plastic, and 7 is for the rest. It is a tricky middle where many plastics are lumped together.

quiz.p: A computer sorts photographs of people, and a researcher fears it makes more mistakes on one group than another. How can she find out?
opts: Count both kinds of mistake separately for each group
quiz.why: An overall count can hide differences between groups. Counting each group separately is how uneven mistakes were found in face-sorting systems.

quiz.p: Which job can a computer do that a person with a ruler and paper cannot easily do?
opts: Make a cut-off that is right for everyone
Find clumps among hundreds of numbers at once
quiz.why: A person can draw a map of two numbers. A computer can look for clumps among hundreds. But people still choose the numbers and decide what the clumps mean.

quiz.p: Putting things in order by a number gives a ____.
quiz.why: A ladder lines things up from the smallest to the biggest number. A cut-off then splits it into groups.

open_questions.q: Are the groups we find on maps in nature, or are they made by the numbers we choose?
open_questions.why_open: Some groups, such as all the atoms of one element, do not depend on what we measure. For many others, such as star types, species or kinds of plastic, scientists and philosophers still argue about how much of the group belongs to the world and how much belongs to the way we look.

open_questions.q: Can a computer find groups that no person has ever thought of, and will we understand them?
open_questions.why_open: Computers already find clumps in huge piles of numbers, such as weather, galaxies and shopping. Whether the groups they find always mean something we can explain is not settled.

open_questions.q: Can a sorter ever make no mistakes at all?
open_questions.why_open: When the two groups overlap on every number we can measure, no sorter can be perfect. Whether new measurements can always pull groups apart is not known.

open_questions.q: Are there kinds of material that nobody has made, in the empty parts of the materials chart?
open_questions.why_open: Some empty parts of the chart are empty because no material can do that. Others are empty only because nobody has found a way yet. It is hard to tell which is which.

open_questions.q: Why do languages draw the lines between colours at different places?
open_questions.why_open: Some researchers think the colour words come from how our eyes work, and others think they come from culture and what people need to say. Studies in different peoples' languages have found some of each.

open_questions.q: How should a sorter choose between a mistake that costs a little and one that costs a lot?
open_questions.why_open: The cost of each kind of mistake is a choice about values, not a fact of science. People disagree about it for fire alarms, medical tests and exams.

maths.problem: A ladder of foods has these katori masses in grams: 60, 80, 80, 95, 100, 105, 120, 120, 128 and 180. Heavy means at or above the cut-off. How many foods are heavy with a cut-off of 100? With a cut-off of 110? With a cut-off of 125? Which foods change group when the cut-off moves from 100 to 125?
maths.answer: 6 foods, then 4 foods, then 2 foods. The foods of 100, 105, 120 and 120 grams change group.
maths.explain: At 100 grams, the foods of 100, 105, 120, 120, 128 and 180 are heavy, which is 6. At 110 grams, 120, 120, 128 and 180 are heavy, which is 4. At 125 grams, 128 and 180 are heavy, which is 2. Between 100 and 125, the foods of 100, 105, 120 and 120 grams move from heavy to light.
maths.context: In the Katori Map test, you line up ten foods by the mass of a katori and draw a cut-off line. Here are made-up masses.
maths.why_maths: Counting how many things fall on each side of a cut-off shows how the choice of line changes the groups, and which things never move.

maths.problem: In the strict round, 11 out of 20 toor dal were wrongly kept back. In the relaxed round, 11 out of 20 chana dal were wrongly let through. What percentage is each? Which round made fewer mistakes in total, if the strict round also let 0 chana through and the relaxed round also kept 1 toor dal back?
maths.answer: 55 percent each. The strict round made fewer mistakes: 11 compared with 12.
maths.explain: 11 out of 20 is 55 out of 100, which is 55 percent. The strict round had 11 plus 0, which is 11 mistakes. The relaxed round had 11 plus 1, which is 12 mistakes. So the strict round made 1 fewer.
maths.context: In the Strict or Relaxed test, you sort a mix of toor dal and chana dal twice, and count the two kinds of mistake. These are made-up numbers.
maths.why_maths: Percentages let you compare mistakes out of different totals, and adding the two kinds shows the total cost of a sorter.

maths.problem: A rice mill counts a stone let through as 10 points of cost, and a good grain thrown out as 1 point. In every 1000 grains, the strict setting throws out 30 good grains and lets 0 stones through. The loose setting throws out 2 good grains and lets 1 stone through. What is the cost of each setting for 5000 grains?
maths.answer: The strict setting costs 150 points. The loose setting costs 60 points.
maths.explain: For 1000 grains, strict costs 30 times 1, which is 30 points. Loose costs 2 times 1 plus 1 times 10, which is 12 points. For 5000 grains, multiply by 5. Strict is 30 times 5, which is 150 points. Loose is 12 times 5, which is 60 points.
maths.why_maths: Giving each kind of mistake a cost lets you add them up and compare two sorters, instead of counting mistakes as if they were all the same.

maths.problem: On your map, flour is at 80 grams and 48 millimetres, maida is at 80 grams and 51 millimetres, rice is at 120 grams and 31 millimetres, and poha is at 60 grams and 40 millimetres. Which food sits closest to flour? How many millimetres lower is the rice heap than the flour heap?
maths.answer: Maida sits closest. The rice heap is 17 millimetres lower.
maths.explain: Maida has the same mass as flour, 80 grams, and is only 3 millimetres higher. The others differ in both numbers. 48 take away 31 is 17. So the rice heap is 17 millimetres lower than the flour heap.
maths.context: In the Katori Map test, each food is a dot with a mass across and a heap height up. Here are made-up numbers for four foods.
maths.why_maths: Reading a map means reading two numbers for each dot and comparing both, which is how you decide whether two dots are close.

maths.problem: Five toor dal pieces are 4, 5, 5, 6 and 6 millimetres wide. Five chana dal pieces are 5, 6, 7, 7 and 8 millimetres wide. A slot lets a piece fall through if the piece is narrower than the slot. For slots of 4.5, 5.5, 6.5 and 7.5 millimetres, count the mistakes in each. A mistake is a toor dal that does not fall through, or a chana dal that does. Which slot is best?
maths.answer: 4.5 gives 4 mistakes, 5.5 gives 3, 6.5 gives 2 and 7.5 gives 4. The 6.5 millimetre slot is best.
maths.explain: At 4.5, one toor dal falls through and 4 are kept back, and no chana falls, so 4 mistakes. At 5.5, three toor dal fall through, 2 are kept back, and 1 chana falls, so 3 mistakes. At 6.5, all 5 toor dal fall, and 2 chana fall, so 2 mistakes. At 7.5, all toor fall, and 4 chana fall, so 4 mistakes. The best slot makes 2 mistakes. No slot makes none, because the sizes overlap.
maths.context: In the Slot Sorter challenge, you build a sorter with a gap and count both kinds of mistake. These are made-up widths.
maths.why_maths: Counting the mistakes for each slot shows the trade-off between the two kinds, and finds the best cut-off even when no cut-off is perfect.

maths.problem: A spice shop has 24 jars. The owner splits them into 2 groups, then splits each of those into 3 groups, then splits each of those into 2 groups. How many small groups are there at the end? How many jars are in each, if the groups are the same size?
maths.answer: 12 small groups, with 2 jars in each.
maths.explain: 2 times 3 is 6, and 6 times 2 is 12. So there are 12 small groups. 24 jars shared among 12 groups is 24 divided by 12, which is 2 jars each.
maths.context: In the Lumpers and Splitters activity, you sort spices into groups and then split the groups into smaller groups.
maths.why_maths: Each split multiplies the number of groups, so multiplying shows how fast the groups grow when you sort at finer levels.

maths.problem: After a relaxed round, there are 30 pieces in the toor bowl and 11 of them are chana dal. If you pick one piece from the bowl with your eyes closed, what is the chance that it is chana dal? Is that more or less than half?
maths.answer: 11 out of 30. That is less than half.
maths.explain: There are 30 pieces, and 11 of them are chana dal, so the chance is 11 out of 30. Half of 30 is 15. 11 is less than 15, so the chance is less than half.
maths.context: In the Strict or Relaxed test, the toor bowl after a relaxed round holds some chana dal that does not belong. These are made-up numbers.
maths.why_maths: A chance shows how often a bowl will contain a wrong piece, which tells you how much to trust the bowl.

maths.problem: In the Star Map, 16 stars are plotted. Four of them are giants and 1 is a white dwarf. The rest lie on the main sequence. How many stars are on the main sequence? What fraction of all the stars is that?
maths.explain: 4 giants plus 1 white dwarf is 5 stars. 16 take away 5 is 11. So 11 of the 16 stars lie on the main sequence. That is more than half, because half of 16 is 8.
maths.context: In the Star Map activity, you plot sixteen stars by colour and brightness and ring the clumps.
maths.why_maths: A fraction tells you how big a family is compared with all the stars, which shows how common the main sequence is.

maths.problem: Five voters draw the line between soft and hard at rungs 4, 5, 5, 6 and 8 of a ladder of ten things. Find the average rung. Which rung is in the middle when they are in order? Which of the two is a better description of where most voters put the line, and why?
maths.answer: The average is 5.6 and the middle rung is 5. The middle rung describes most voters better.
maths.explain: 4 plus 5 plus 5 plus 6 plus 8 is 28, and 28 divided by 5 is 5.6. In order, the rungs are 4, 5, 5, 6, 8, and the middle one is 5. The voter at 8 pulls the average up, but most voters are at 5 or 6, so the middle rung is closer to what most voters did.
maths.context: In the Soft or Hard test, five voters put things in order and draw a line between soft and hard. These are made-up results.
maths.why_maths: An average and a middle value can differ when one voter is far from the rest, and knowing both helps you describe where a group of people put a line.

roots.context: We have sorted things by lines and by maps. Now we ask what sorting tells us about the world, and about the one who sorts.

deep_truth.truth: Laid out by one number, the foods made a ladder with no gaps. Every line we drew on it was our choice. Laid out by two numbers, some foods fell into clumps with empty space between them. A gap belongs to the numbers we chose, as well as to the foods.
deep_truth.habit: We say that these foods are one kind, as if the group sat inside the foods. But the same foods can fall into other groups when we measure other numbers, so a group is partly a fact about our measuring.
deep_truth.evidence: On the Katori Map, which foods formed a clump depended on the two numbers we plotted. On the mass ladder alone, there was no clear gap, so every cut-off was a choice. If your map shows no clear clumps, that tells you something too: those two numbers do not split these foods.

three.who_am_i: You are a dot on many maps at once, such as your height, your age and your marks. On each map you sit in a different clump, and no clump is the whole of you.
three.what_is_life: Your body sorts all the time. Your tongue sorts sweet from bitter, and your gut sorts what to keep from what to pass on. Every sorter in a body makes some mistakes, and the body lives with them.
three.what_is_this_world: Nature has real patterns, such as the gap between white dwarfs and bright stars. The boxes and the names are ours, and a new number can show a new pattern.

roots.thread: Start with one heap of foods. One number puts the heap in a line. Two numbers spread the heap into a flat picture, where clumps may show. More numbers can show more. At every step the heap is the same heap. The groups come from looking, and the looking is done by someone who is part of the same world as the heap.

teachings.teaching: In this Buddhist text, blind men each touch a different part of an elephant and say what an elephant is. One touches the head, one the tail, one the leg. They argue, and each is right about the part they touched.
teachings.link: One number is like one part of the elephant. A second number shows more, and neither one alone tells you what the whole heap is.

teachings.teaching: Zhuangzi says that 'this' and 'that' give birth to each other. Without a 'that' there is no 'this'.
teachings.link: When you draw a cut-off, 'heavy' and 'light' are born at the same moment. Neither group exists before the line.

teachings.teaching: Rivers that flow east and rivers that flow west all go to the sea and become the sea. Once they are in the sea, they do not know 'I am this river, I am that river'.
teachings.link: The names we give to groups are like the names of rivers. They are useful on the way, and they all belong to one heap.

science.text: On a map of brightness against colour, stars fall into families: the main sequence, the giants and the white dwarfs.
Whether the groups that scientists find are in nature, or are partly made by the numbers they choose to measure, is argued by philosophers of science.

other_view.who: Many scientists and philosophers who think some groups are real
other_view.view: Some groups do not depend on our numbers. Every atom of gold is exactly like every other, and no atom sits half way to silver. An element is not a line that we drew. Where we find groups like that, the clumps were there before we measured.

how_we_found_out.story: About 1900, astronomers at Harvard College Observatory sorted thousands of stars by the dark lines in their light. Annie Jump Cannon led the sorting, and Antonia Maury added careful notes on how sharp the lines were. These were two ladders: a type, and a brightness. Around 1905, a Danish astronomer named Ejnar Hertzsprung noticed that among the red stars, some were enormously bright and others very faint, with few in between. In 1913, the American astronomer Henry Norris Russell showed brightness against type for many stars on one map. The stars were not scattered everywhere. Most lay along a long band, with bright giants above it and faint white dwarfs below. For a while, many thought the map showed the path that every star travels as it ages. That turned out to be wrong. Later, physics showed that the band is made of stars of different masses, all burning hydrogen. One map had shown the families before anybody knew why they existed.
how_we_found_out.who: Ejnar Hertzsprung (Danish) and Henry Norris Russell (American), using the sorting by Annie Jump Cannon and Antonia Maury
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Many thought that the band of stars on the map was a path that every star follows as it ages, from giant to dwarf. Later work showed that stars of different masses sit at different places on the band, and that each star stays near one place for most of its life.
